[h1] What 1000 hours of Dark Souls 2 does to an mf [/h1]

So, Dark Souls 2 is on sale, I have now hit 1000 hours of playtime on it, and you're wondering whether you should buy it or not. Here's the short answer, as someone who is obsessed with this game:
[b] YES. [/b]
Now here's the longer answer. Dark Souls 2 is a game with very clearly defined strengths and weaknesses; things it does very well and things it doesn't do well.

[u] THE GOOD: [/u]
[list]
    [*]Lots of content. Sh*t-tons of it. This is easily the biggest, longest, and most content packed of all the Souls games.
    [*]Great game balance and viability. With very few exceptions, almost every playstyle and build you can think of is viable.
    [*]Huge build diversity. Due to the previous points, there's an enormous amount of builds, weapons, spells, and playstyles to try out. With 1000 hours in the game, I'm still enjoying trying new combinations and builds.
    [*]Deliberate and methodic combat. Every swing, spell cast, roll, and block is a proper commitment. How and when you use these massively decide the outcome of a fight.
    [*]Excellent online mechanics for both PvP and Co-op. You can duel and co-op in any area regardless of bosses being alive, revive bosses to fight over and over for secret loot and more souls, and enter a host of covenants with very unique online mechanics from reverse-invading hosts into your world to free-for-all invasions in challenge areas where both hosts and invaders can heal.
    [*]A unique NG+ experience that sets itself apart from all other Souls games by having new enemies, invaders, events, armour, weapons, spells, etc.
[/list]

[u] THE BAD: [/u]
[list]
    [*]Nerfed tracking and introduction of sweet-spot mechanic on certain weapons makes combat notably more difficult to get used to and master than other Souls games.
    [*]Difficulty of areas and bosses can vary a lot. Sometimes bosses and areas are simple and of no particular difficulty and sometimes they can be absolutely brutal.
    [*]Soul Memory mechanic. It (essentially) causes you to always be roughly matched with people at the same stage of game/playthrough progression, which can make it hard to play with friends and strangers who are considerably before/further than your progression.
[/list]

For me, this game is all about the combat and builds. That's why I like it so much, and that's why I've been playing it for 1000 hours without getting bored, and why I'll continue to play it for many more hours to come. There's other things to enjoy as well, like the lore, colourful characters, wide array of armour choices (fashion souls best souls), and unique in-game challenges. 
If this and the previous things sound interesting and good to you, then I absolutely recommend getting this game. Sale or no sale, first Souls game or fourth. Dark Souls 2 is great.

Before I started my Dark Souls 2 journey, I was extremely hesitant to play this game because of the insane amount of negativity around it. I clearly remember googling “Should I skip DS2 and directly play DS3 after DS1?”
I’m writing this for anyone who’s in the same boat.

[b]TLDR:[/b] Yes, the game has issues. No, they’re not as bad as people make them out to be. Most of them are manageable, and if you know about them beforehand, you can still enjoy the game a lot.

[b]Story[/b]
Let’s get this out of the way. Dark Souls 2 is only loosely connected to DS1 and DS3. It takes place in Drangleic, which is probably a different location (or dimension). In that sense, DS3 feels way more like a direct sequel to DS1, and skipping DS2 won’t make you miss much story-wise.

Still, I think you should play DS2 before DS3.

[b]Why DS2 isn’t as bad as people say[/b]
This game is not nearly as terrible as the internet makes it out to be. Once something gets labeled “the bad one,” that reputation just sticks. DS2 doesn’t help itself either, since some core mechanics are poorly explained and easy to misunderstand.

Once you learn how things actually work, there’s a lot to like here. Sadly, the game barely explains any of it, so you’ll probably end up googling stuff. These are the big ones:

[list]
[*][b]Adaptability (ADP)[/b]
This stat is way more important than the game tells you. It affects Agility, which controls roll i-frames and Estus speed. If you’re not using a shield, level this early. At least leveling is fast in DS2.

[*][b]Humanity / Hollowing[/b]
Dying lowers your max HP by 5 percent per death, up to 50 percent. I hate this mechanic. You can fix it with Human Effigies or just wear the Ring of Binding (cuts the penalty to 25 percent and is available early). Also, being undead / hollowed doesn’t stop invasions, so don’t overthink it.

[*][b]Boss gimmicks[/b]
A lot of bosses have gimmicks, and missing them can make fights feel way harder than they should be. The game hides these as “secrets,” which is dumb. Examples:
[list]
[*]Burn the windmill to remove poison from Mytha’s arena (still makes no sense).
[*]Hold a torch during Duke’s Dear Freja so spiders don’t swarm you.
[*]Light up Lost Sinner’s arena before the fight.
[/list]
If a boss feels unfair, just google it. You probably missed something.
[/list]

[b]Stuff you just have to deal with[/b]
Some problems aren’t fixable, you just learn to live with them (and yes, some of these exist in other Souls games too):

[list]
[*][b]Awful boss runbacks[/b]. Executioner’s Chariot and Smelter Demon are especially bad. Also, you might be missing a secret bonfire (fuck secret bonfires).
[*][b]Inconsistent damage[/b]. Damage can feel random because too many things affect it.
[*][b]Enemy placement[/b]. Enemy density is often too high, so you’re constantly fighting groups.
[*][b]Difficulty for the wrong reasons[/b]. Sometimes the game just throws cheap stuff at you to kill you. It’s annoying, not hard.
[/list]

[b]What I actually like[/b]
There is actually a lot to like here, but I won't be spoiling them. You should experience them for yourself. Still I will briefly mention couple of things I loved. Positioning matters a lot, which makes combat feel more tactical. The environments are dark and oppressive in a way that fits Souls perfectly. NG+ actually changes things. The DLCs are excellent and in some cases better than the base game.

[h1] Too Long Didn't Read [/h1]

Graphics improvements are just the icing on the cake.  The real reason to upgrade or buy Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is for the drastically improved [b] core content [/b] and [b] game flow[/b].  DLC and Scholar Bonus content are worked into the game more naturally.  Many issues the community had with the design have been attempted to be addressed via drastic layout changes.

[u] Detailed Review [/u]

[h1] The Controversy [/h1]

Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is a new rendition of Dark Souls II.

There are [b]three major complaints[/b] the community had with this new version that I'd like to address:

[olist]
[*] This is just a minor graphical update that the PC could've handled originally (DirectX 11)

[*] The Dark Souls II community would be split apart on two separate servers.  The old DirectX 9 server and the new DirectX 11 server.

[*] The 60 FPS durability bug. [b]*Update*[/b]
[b]The Developers have acknowledged the durability bug and are planning a fix.[/b]

Source: [url=http://info.darksouls.jp/other/pc/information_detail/2015-04-16-01.html] http://info.darksouls.jp/other/pc/information_detail/2015-04-16-01.html[/url]
[/olist]

Although the existence of this game does split the community, the cost of upgrading for exisiting users is offered at a substantial discount: 
$20 for owners of the previous game who also had the DLC
$30 for owners of the previous game who do not own the DLC

The cost to upgrade is pretty small considering the massive amount of time many players spend playing these Souls games (500+ hours isn't too uncommon).  Multiplayer is very active at pretty much all levels of play at this point on the DirectX 11 version.

[u]A comment on the community split[/u]
If you're having problems with finding multiplayer on the DirectX9 version, I'd definitely recommend considering the upgrade, especially for PC users.  [b]The entire community could arguably reunite and stick with the DirectX11 version.[/b]  It's not expensive and the changes have added variety and a much more fair challenge to all of the game's core areas.  

If you're worried about having to make a new character and start from scratch, I guarantee you it won't take as long as you think.  [b]You might even enjoy the fresh new playthrough(s)[/b] as much as I have.

[u]A comment on the graphics[/u]:
The contrast between light and dark has improved.  Torches and spell effects look better.  [b]This is not the reason to get the game though.[/b]


[h1] The Real Reason to buy or upgrade to Scholar of the First Sin [/h1]

Many forum posts I read discussing this game were very focused on the DirectX11 graphics and how this game was just reselling slightly upgraded graphics and nothing else.

[b] The real reason to pick up this new version is for the massive amount of changes made to the core adventure.[/b]  What do I mean?

*Semi-Spoilers*
The developers/designers have stepped through [b]every single area in the original game[/b] and made massive revisions to:

[olist]
[*][spoiler] Placement, amount and type of enemies.  You'll find new, area appropriate enemies all over the place that weren't originally there before. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Some enemies have been removed or reduced from their original locations entirely. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] There are some new NPCs you can summon to your aid that are running some pretty cool builds.  The placement of some old NPC summon signs have also been adjusted to make those NPCs more useful in their respective areas. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Many Major items and upgrades have been moved around drastically. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Barriers are erected in areas you wouldn't expect. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Shortcuts added in other places. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Thankfully this version removes the free preorder bonus weapons that are automatically handed out to every character you create (making starting equipment slightly more meaningful).  Don't worry, they can still be purchased for souls at a certain vendor, deeper within the game. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] The DLC areas can't just be immediately accessed for free any more.  You must earn the right to enter each DLC area by finding the appropriate keys in very lore appropriate locations within the game. [/spoiler]

[*][spoiler] Many, Many, new invasions.  Some of which are random.[/spoiler]
[/olist]

[b]The actual line-by-line changelist for Scholar of the First Sin is so massive that it would take too long for me to list it all here.[/b]  

Just know that [b]every area that is not part of the DLC has undergone substantial changes.[/b]  

You should just experience it for yourself.  Reddit was trying to list all of the changes and the list just runs for pages long.


[h1] What do all these changes mean? [/h1] 

If all you wanted out of a Souls game is the story and you've played Dark Souls II already, there's nothing new to see here. (Unless you haven't played the DLC and the Scholar content...)

If you like Dark Souls for the adventure, the multiplayer and the encounters though, this update is definitely for you.  The revisions made to this game result in an [b]extremely polished gameplay experience.[/b]

It's very obvious that careful thought was put into these revisions to make certain areas more enjoyable to play through.

Scholar of the First Sin was more fun to play through than the DirectX 9 version as a result of these content changes.


[h1] The DLC: The Lost Crowns + the Scholar of the First Sin Bonus Content [/h1]

Quick note on the DLC since there are some people who may have played the main game but not the DLC yet.

The DLC has excellent level design / bosses and supplements the story very well.  Each area also introduces some really cool and unique equipment that can help spruce up your character's fighting style or utility.  The designers may have very well used what they learned from building the DLC to help make the original game flow better.

Ultimately, Scholar of the First Sin does a great job at [b] naturally [/b] working the DLC and Scholar Bonus content into the game [b]in a way that feels natural.[/b]  They don't feel tacked on like in the DirectX9 version.



When you look at this new game as a whole, it offers a gargantuan amount of real estate to explore, co-op and pvp in.  Many of the changes that were made to the game, could only have been made after analyzing the community response to the original version of Dark Souls II and watching how regular users play the game via online streams. 

[b]Tremendous Value, Highest Recommendation[/b]

Here's how you play Dark Souls II:
1. Buy game on sale or for the full price.
2. Beat at least 3 bosses.
3. Lose patience over the stupidly annoying enemies.
4. Take a year break.
5. Come back to the game as a veteran soulsborne player.
6. Start a new DS2 run.
7. Actually start enjoying DS2.
8. Finish game and realize what you missed out on.
After 62.7h of attempts, I beat the first boss "The pursuer", I just hope I don't find more bosses like that. I feel very close to the end of the game!

Don't be a fool and listen to people who've barely played the game. A lot of them only complain about it not working like DS1 and DS3, whereas it tries to be a completely different game, let me tell you how different.

It's animations are smoother, even if slower. Most if not all animations aren't choppy unlike DS3 and especially DS1.

It's actually optimized. Believe or or not, DS2 has the best PC port out of any of the souls games. It will run on most systems even dated ones. The only real requirement happens to be 64-Bit Windows. Should hardly be a hassle to get, no? Keyboard and Mouse work about as well as Controllers if not sometimes better. I recommend going to settings and control mapping everything to suit your needs. The base controls aren't the best and if you're going to use mouse to do ANYTHING other than camera movement and lock-on. I urge you to disable Double-Clicking.

It does not sugarcoat its areas. DS2 has many areas and many more bosses. The land this game takes place in, Drangleic, has been said to have a great military might. And the game shows it perfectly. It has powerful enemies, and in places you would hardly expect when going on a first run. Some areas may prove more dangerous than the boss of the area. Which some think is a detriment. Which, while I understand. I urge you to realize the Souls Series aren't purely boss-fighting games. Appreciate the areas and their enemies. Don't just bias on the bosses.

It has genuine variety. DS2 has like what? Around 100 or so armour sets I think? Sounds about right, and you can mix and match all of them. Splendid is it not? But hold on, that's not the only variety. Weapons, you can use all of them with viability. Unlike your other two games where some weapons are clearly superior in every single way - or the inverse, DS2 makes it possible for you to use ANY weapon and dish out damage while enjoying yourself. Plus despite nerfs, magic is also tremendously viable in this game. You can make yourself to be ANY build and have fun with it. Heck, even on SL1 you can do some fun things that wouldn't be possible for the other games.

Lets also talk about something else: POWERSTANCING! With the correct stats you are able to powerstance two weapons. What does this mean? And how to do it? Well you just hold your two-handing button. As for what it means, you will use TWO weapons at the same time. With a new unique moveset.
Just remember to have 1.5x the Stat Requirements of the weapons you're wielding. Both of them. Else you'll just wield your left hand weapon with two hands.

I also wish to mention the PvP in this game is stellar. Unlike both the other games this game also has itself well optimized to having a good PvP session. Same goes for Co-op. And unlike DS3, it also handles Ganks quite a bit better. Whenever a player with phantoms is invaded, the phantoms will have their estus disabled. As for the PvP aspect, learn the weapons, master the weapons. All of them can be viable if you know how to use them.

I'll also put in a quick mention that DS2 has the most intricately designed mechanics out of any of the souls games. And most of them, aren't badly done. I.E. Weight affecting fall damage, stamina recovery, roll distance, and I think even run speed. That's a good mechanic. There are of course others that are not, and I will get to them.

Soul Memory system for example. How bad is it? Before, not so much. But with the introduction of the Agape Ring which is very cheap to obtain. It became horrendous. The Soul Memory system would inevitably lock players from "twinking" - meaning using late-game fully upgraded gear against early-game players. Only the cheap agape ring makes it so "twinking" is fully possible again. Of course players can also pass down items from a late-game character to an early-game one. But still, the Agape Ring simply makes everything easier does it not?

Adaptability. It's a great concept but badly implemented. Adaptability raises Agility, which in turn raises the speed of which you use items, and the amount of i-frames your character has. We here recommend raising it until you have about 96 Agility. Or 99-100 is a fine number as well to stop at. With 100 also increasing backstep i-frames. [Which is great for PvP.]
It's badly implemented because, well it doesn't make the game very friendly to new players. Especially those who don't like to read the info for each stat. And this isn't the 'very friendly' where your hand is held through danger that I'm talking about. I'm saying it somewhat is an artificial difficulty.

Bosses. Well, I have to admit, a lot of the bosses do lack flavour. While others are contenders for best Souls Boss. Which is a bit like the other games in some regards but DS2 has a good few bosses which are a bit on the 'eh' side. Most of them early-game bosses, and about one or two late-game bosses. The DLC bosses aside from 2 optional ones, are VERY GOOD.carving. So look forward to doing those.

And lastly, it can be easy to get lost. While there are many paths, most of them are linear and don't connect to an earlier area. Meaning you can easily get lost in them thinking maybe there's more to do and what not. Of course, players coming from DS3 will have no issue because DS3 is more linear than Pokemon games. Those coming from DS1 though, yeah. Just remember most if not all paths, don't lead back to an earlier area. While you're here, light all those primal bonfires will ya? Those are the ones you find after beating a Great One and taking their soul.

If you require ANY help at all. Join the Dark Souls discord and hop onto the Drangleic channel. Unlike DS3 and DS1 channels, we're willing to help any new players, and we also appreciate co-op play quite a bit. See you around Undead! Have a good death!

A common viewpoint of the Souls community seems to be how horrifically bad Dark Souls 2 is, however personally I can't agree. There are certainly some stark differences between 1 and 2; a lot of things were changed, and while I like some there are others that I dislike, so let's get right into the details.

Soul Memory based matchmaking; possibly the biggest criticism of Dark Souls 2, and it's a mechanic I'm not that fond of. In short, Soul Memory is a count of every single soul your character has received over the course of its life. Obviously, this can present a bit of a problem. For instance; a SL100 character can have a 10 million SM in his record by simply choosing to end his character progression at 100, meanwhile someone who continued to level can also have a 10 million SM while instead being SL250.

The only other mechanic I'm not entirely fond of is Agility. Unlike in 1, the amount of iFrames you have on your roll is dependent upon stats; namely your Agility stat which can be increased both by putting points into Attunement or Adaptability. Baseline Agility (which depends upon starting class) is going to be either 85 or 86, and at 85 you only get 5 iFrames on your roll whereas at 86 you have 8 iFrames. Meanwhile once your Adaptability and/or Attunement have been leveled up sufficiently so that you reach 116 Agility you will have 16 iFrames on your roll.

Now for a change I'm actually fond of; namely losing health upon death. Every time you die in Dark Souls 2 you'll lose 5% of your maximum HP. This health degradation caps out at 50% of maximum health, or 80% if you've got the Ring of Binding equipped. This is a mechanic that I completely love, because it truly punishes you for death. In Dark Souls 1 the only punishment you have for death is having to retrieve your souls as well as losing your Human status, which only reduces your status resistances somewhat, and while you do lose your Ember in 3 for death (causing a 25% loss of health) there's no penalty for continued deaths unless you pop another Ember.

Why do I love this mechanic? Because I feel that it makes death more threatening than in the other two games. Potentially losing your souls permanently is threatening, yes, however If you had little souls to begin with then death is nearly meaningless. In 2, however, each time you die you're able to take 5% less damage before dying once more. Because of this I feel the game somewhat forces you to learn from your mistakes better than either of the other Dark Souls games, and this being a Souls game, that's something that I feel everyone should love. All of us do so love to die, after all.

Dual wielding is another thing that Dark Souls 2 did exceptionally well. While 1 had no dual wield system to speak of and 3 changed the system to a much more inferior version of 2's system, the power stance mechanic in 2 is excellent. To explain, if you have 1.5x the stat requirements of the weapons in both your right and left hands you can hold down the two hand key (which would normally two hand your left handed weapon) to enter power stance. When in power stance your left handed light attack key will change to be a combo attack with both weapons, while the left handed heavy attack button will now do a power attack with both weapons.

The reason I love this mechanic so much is that you can power stance nearly any weapon combo so long as you have the required stats to do so. This gives quite a lot of freedom in your weapon setup, especially when one considers how limited the dual weapons in 3 are (namely, there's a grand total of, I believe, 6 in the entire game). The weapon combos people can come up with are mostly limited to their creativity and what they want their ending build to be.

Speaking of ending build, another positive feature of 2; Soul Vessels. In Dark Souls 1 there is no method of changing your stats, whereas in 3 you're limited to 5 respecs each NG cycle via Rosaria. In 2 you can respec at any time by giving a Soul Vessel to Strowen in Things Betwixt. If the player is being thorough they will receive a good number of Soul Vessels in each NG cycle, meaning that they can respec with a large amount of freedom. Additionally, the Bonfire Ascetic item is a unique aspect to 2.

Bonfire Ascetics are items that 'reset' a specific zone around a bonfire by putting it into the NG state directly above the one that zone is currently in. When this happens all enemies, corpse-bound items, and wooden chest items are respawned, whereas metal chests are not. This allows you to either farm bosses for their souls to get every item from said soul, to farm specific items in that zone, or to simply soul farm from either the boss of the zone of the normal enemies.

New Game Plus, AKA NG+ is done better in 2 than the other games. Various red phantom versions of enemies are added in, some replace normal enemies and some are simply added to the zone. Additionally, the chests which are mimics are changed from base NG. In Dark Souls 1 NG+ only adds health and damage to enemies, so naturally this is change I utterly love. The 'lazy' NG+ was always my far biggest complaint of Dark Souls 1 and 3, as I didn't feel the changes they made were really enough.

Achievement Hunting; and why would I include this? Purely for personal reasons. No other game have I enjoyed quite so much to specifically go out of my way to hunt down every achievement in the game. However, I wanted 100% achievements in Dark Souls 2. While this likely has little to no meaning to anyone else, this to me shows just how much I enjoy the game, and thus it deserves mention.

The last positive I have is the DLC's as well as the Scholar of the First Sin edition. Scholar of the First Sin is an extremely well done 'reskin' of the base Dark Souls 2. Numerous items had their placements changed to locations that, in my opinion, are more fitting, enemies have been adjusted to make the game more enjoyable, and overall it's a great upgrade. Additionally, the three DLCs (Crown of the Sunken King, Crown of the Old Iron King, Crown of the Old Ivory King) are hands down AMAZING.

Make no mistake; Dark Souls 2 itself is an excellent game, however the quality of the DLCs is simply excellent and I cannot say enough good things about the DLCs. Each of the three DLCs are by and far more difficult than most of the non-DLC content, however this is done in a good way. I'm not going to explain further as it's impossible to prevent spoiling the DLC, but suffice to say the experience of playing the DLCs the first time is nothing short of amazing.

I've went on about a lot of positives so far, but for the final note I'm going to talk about covenants. For the most part I'm neutral on the covenants in 2, however I do have one negative; the lack of the Blade of the Darkmoon covenant. I'm aware that the Blue Sentinels are in 2 and that they serve essentially the same purpose as the Darkmoons in 3, however the Darkmoons were always my favorite in 1, as was the buff Darkmoon Blade that you get from them, and the absence of both said covenant and miracle is something I can't simply ignore.

All in all I'm possibly going to be the only person you'll ever hear say that Dark Souls 2 is their favorite installment in the series, and I'm fully aware that I'm the holder of a greatly unpopular opinion with that. As with anything the game is not without its flaws, some of them larger than others. However on a whole it's a great game. A must play for anyone that considers themselves a Souls veteran and, at least in my personal opinion, an excellent game for anyone new to the Souls franchise.

If I had to give a numerical rating it would be a 9/10. While it's not a perfect and with some mechanics I'm not fond of Dark Souls 2 is, in my opinion, the best overall game of the Souls series. I know it's a lot of text, but hopefully this helps at least a few people make the choice to play Dark Souls 2.

Don't hate this game simply because it's different from what you've expected. An unloved child of the trilogy, justifying its fate by the circumstances of its creation. It's full of experiments, discoveries and surprises. But most importantly, it's still Souls, even though some rules may have changed. If you still think that this is the worst Souls game, it may still be one of the greatest games on its own. So don't skip it, give it a try.

The single thing that you need to know beforehand, it's adaptability (and agility). It's the one thing that can break your experience. So level it up a bit and things will go smoother.

It takes off with a rough start. You are at your weakest and even your reflexes and memory may fail you. Have patience and take it slowly. It's a huge world that will show you all its wonders if you are ready to perceive. Oh how many wonders does it have...

It's a very long and ambitious game, with a huge arsenal of weapons, places and enemies. The variety of places to go, the variety of weapons and mechanics, everything is possible. Whatever you choose, there is no wrongs. Be whoever you want to be, look whatever you want to look like and do whatever you want. It's your own choice and your own story. [i]Isn't it wonderful?[/i]

You can re-fight your favorite bosses multiple times or exterminate every living creature in the wilds for good. You can accept additional hardships by joining a certain covenant. You can use two weapons at once if you can't choose which one of them you like most. And if you seek something new, than the new game plus will surely give you some surprises.

I love this world. How huge, diverse and charming it is. Every time I stepped into a new location, I stopped to admire the scenery. The places might lack some bonds, but they are marvelous on their own. The darkness of the deepest pits, the cruelty of blizzards, the splendor of dragons in the sky, the sadness of abandoned halls... And the hopeful peace of Majula. 

I will never consider it the worst. It will always have its place in my heart together, as equals, with other soulsborne games. Even if it may have some flaws (no thing in this world is perfect!), it shines brighter in other aspects. And for this shining, for this unique flame - it is worth to bear this curse.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]

The 'Soul' series is known for harsh difficulty and rewarding gameplay in which dying is mostly the players' own fault for making a wrong move at the wrong time.

In difference to many modern RPGs the lore is kind of hidden as well as it's neither presented in amazing cutscenes nor illuminated from every perspective. 
The player has to actually read dialogues and item descriptions, revealing piece by piece of the backgrounds and the story. 

In 'Dark Souls II' the main recipe of the series stays the same: A lonesome traveler in a kingdom (haunted by an undead curse) starts a journey full of fighting, exploring and dying. The player will get crushed by hammers and axes, pierced by spears and arrows, cut by daggers and swords, melted by fireballs, cursed by hexes-... there are definitely lots of ways to die and you have to face all of them if you want to survive and see the end of your journey.

There are many negative aspects that stick to 'Dark Souls II' since its release. Many of them are still somewhat present but with the three DLCs, the 'SOTFS' edition and several patches many aspects have changed. I don't want to make another huge review about the game's content (you could easily fill several pages about lore, characters and stuff), so I'll make it 'short' (well okay - it's still quite long) and focus on some main points that bothered me in many reviews.
__________________________________________

[h1]Some say the game is too easy compared to 'Demon's Souls' or 'Dark Souls'…[/h1]

The changed enemy positions in the 'SOTFS' edition and the great levels of the DLCs shall provide some nice challenging experiences for anybody. From my point of view the difficulty level has the right balance between 'challenging‘ and 'frustrating‘. Sure there are some annoying parts, some ganking and some cheap deaths, but it never feels too easy or so hard that I think I may never be able to do it. Even the 'Fume Knight' and the 'Frigid Outskirts' are manageable. And for players who still think it's a piece of cake: Fortunately there is a convenant for you mad ones that increases the overall difficulty even more.
__________________________________________

[h1]Some say the game is ugly…[/h1]

The 'Soul' series was never known for the best graphics of the generation but all the time the overall picture was great and the 'charming' atmosphere made you forget about some of these muddy textures. 'Dark Souls II: SOTFS' is not breaking with this 'rule' but the improved graphics of the 'SOTFS' edition are definitely a good improvement and especially armors are now very detailled. (However with texture modding and ENB and stuff you were able to get nearly the same results out of the original 'Dark Souls II')

The varied landscape in combination with huge buildings and massive monuments of the past (and several nice particle effects) really creates some admirable places where you are able to forget the hopelessness of your journey and immerge into Drangleic – at least until an invader stabs you.
__________________________________________

[h1]Some say the game is not worthy of the 'Souls' series as it feels empty and without the special feeling of its precursors...[/h1]

They say it's no real 'Souls' game, just something else. Sure it’s neither Allant nor Gwyn, neither Boletaria nor Lordran. However Drangleic has several memorable moments, names and characters as well. The story and the lore are atmospheric and well done and I get nearly the same feeling as in the other games. Especially the DLC stories and areas are totally brilliant. They could be imagined as different Archstones and small parts of the world that create an exquisite overall picture, be it the Brume Tower or Frozen Eleum Loyce. 
__________________________________________

I'm a huge fan of the 'Souls‘ series and I've spent several hundreds of hours in the different games: I‘ve visited Boletaria and fought with King Allant, walked in the Valley of Defilement and felt like a demon myself after killing Garl Vinland and the Saint Astraea. I’ve travelled through the holy city of Anor Londo, met the former Lord of Sunlight and brought peace to the legendary knight Artorias and the darkness known as Manus in a time and world long forgotten... 

The 'Souls' games were always full of memorable moments and from my point of view 'Dark Souls II' is no exception in this category: On the top of the castle I fought the Mirror Knight under a rainy sky, I’ve challenged the proud samurai Sir Alonne in a duel and travelled to a castle sunken in a sea of fire - At the end I was finally able to meet a king who has lost everything.
It was definitely a remarkable journey.
__________________________________________

[h1]Cons[/h1]
 
In comparison to the precursors some decisions and changes aren't entirely positive, like e.g. the high amount of bonfires, the immediate teleportation ability or the simplified upgrade system. Some parts of this old 'gloomy desperation' and helplessness that haunted you in the other games are missing - but there are also positive changes that improve the gaming experience: The 'SL1 invader twinks', the 'Dark Wood Grain Ring' rolling (a.k.a. the Ninja Flip) and the lag-stabbing insanity of 'Dark Souls' are nearly gone, respecing your character is now possible and the sheer amount of different weapons, spells, armors and items (Fashion Souls!) is simply amazing and enables many different builds and styles. In addition some of the items that had to be farmed for long hours in the Original 'Dark Souls II' (e.g. Visible Aurous Set) can now be aquired more easily in chests and treasures. 

And above all... since 'Dark Souls II' the game finally features beards - praise the sun for this milestone! \[T]/
__________________________________________

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]

From my point of view make the changes of the 'SOTFS'-Edition the games' atmosphere and lore more coherent and provide challenging new fights and changed enemy positions. 
The DLCs of 'Dark Souls II' are simply amazing and provide exactly what Souls veterans are looking for: fantastic levels with shortcuts and hidden paths, new interesting stories with remarkable characters and challenges from which even the toughest veteran may burst into tears. 

Still 'Dark Souls II‘ is not perfect and overall more a Titanite Chunk than a Titanite Slab. However it’s still damn good and keeps me interested even after over 100 hours. It’s probably an 8.5 out of 10 - well at least if your nerves and your will are strong enough. 

So in the end… it is time to meet your fate Bearer of the Curse. Take a last look at the bonfire, your last anchor in this sea of darkness. Pick up your sword and your shield and move on into the unknown. And never forget your Estus flask…

...you’ll need it. Trust me.

Dark Souls II is what people described the first Dark Souls to be.

Most problems people have with the game can be boiled down to not wanting to fully engage in the first place. People will say "Dark Souls II is a good game, but a bad Dark Souls game" and then purposefully play it as if it's not a Dark Souls game by trying to sprint past every enemy. I agree that they leaned a bit hard into the difficulty for the sake of being difficult, but you can't deny that FromSoft was just responding to the fans apparent love for difficulty that at times felt unfair. Dark Souls fans made their bed and realized they lacked the strength to lay in it. This game is a great game AND a great Dark Souls game, I'd even argue it's more true to the original than DSIII. 

There is still room to critique the game, however most complaints I see are either present in the rest of the trilogy or slander. One of the biggest examples of this is the i-frames regarding the adaptability stat, and this complaint alone can be broken down at multiple points:
1) Dark Souls II gives you more souls per kill for your average enemy and each level up costs you less souls than the other games, so it's not some huge investment people make it out to be
2) The i-frames aren't wrong when you are grabbed by an opponent. Your character is finishing a dodge animation after it was already attacked in the hitbox, and then moves to where the grab connected. There's definitely room to critique visual feedback, but calling the i-frames inaccurate is just wrong (also disingenuous when compared to enemy hitboxes in the other games)
3) I was always confused why people had a problem with Adaptability but not Vitality, but then I played Dark Souls III and saw they kept it. Seems like people are much more lenient when mechanics like this are added to Souls games outside of this one...

With that out of the way, why DO I love this game?

Biggest thing for me is the depth. Even for Dark Souls standards the amount of weapons, armor, rings, etc. and how they all interact together/with the world around you is insane. The game introduces many new mechanics with my favorite being the power stance, which is essentially 2 handing from Elden Ring but with more versatility in weapon choice. Bonfire Ascetics are also a great way to get stronger and grind out more souls/items, or if you just want to fight the area boss again without doing an entire NG+. There are also countless smaller hidden things like a bell helmet that rings when hit in the head, or a pig that helps dig up a pickaxe weapon. With the other 2 games I feel like I have a pretty decent grasp on its mechanics and unique items/quests, while in Dark Souls II I am constantly learning new things.

The story and themes in this game are also unlike the others. Dark Souls II brings a lot more attention to the Undead Curse and how people cope, and while playing the game and seeing the world around me I truly started to feel a hopelessness unlike what I felt in the other games. The NPCs work alongside the theming perfectly to paint a beautifully tragic picture.

I've already written a lot so I just want to finish by saying if you were thinking about skipping over Dark Souls II or if you already have to get to III, I highly recommend you check it out. Don't fall for the propaganda that it's a "Bad Souls Game"

Dark Souls II; where do I start. In the beginning of the game it felt insanely brutal, and by the end it became a cake walk. As someone who has beaten ds3, bb, elden ring, sekiro, and ds1, I can say that ds2 was the most bizarre game with the most obvious flaws. This doesn't at all mean that it is a bad game, on the contrary, I think it some of the highest highs and the lowest lows. 

Firstly, build variety is fantastic in this game. It is significantly better than both ds1 and ds3. I had so much fun using the black knight halberd, the pursuer's ultra greatsword, and finally the fume ultra greatsword. Next playthrough I want to run a miracle build, and I definitely recommend for anyone playing to try to play with a magic build, as having ranged attacks is very useful in certain areas like iron keep, and gives you more content hunting for certain spells.

This game has some very pretty areas, but it does a very poor job connecting them in the same way as ds1 or even ds3. And some of the areas make you question why you are playing the game. The bosses are not difficult almost at all in this game aside from a very few, and the areas are the real challenge. From what I have heard, this is mainly a scholar problem, not a vanilla one. Iron keep, Shrine of Amana, and Undead Crypt were by first the worst areas for me personally. I did not find the Blue Smelter Demon or Sir Alonne's boss runs to be bad. 

The DLCs were great, and I especially liked the Old Iron King and Ivory King DLCs the best (didn't care as much for Sunken Crown). The DLC bosses were significantly higher in quality than the main game ones, and I absolutely recommend doing them. If I were to rank them from best to worst: Ivory King, Old Iron King, Sunken King. Now, the bosses were also really easy from the DLC coming from other souls games, but it doesn't mean they are at all bad. They were all extremely fun to fight. 

Here are a list of problems that the game has: 
- Bad hitboxes 
- Bad balance 
- No immunity on interaction (fog walls) 
- Adaptability (i-frames attached to stats) 
- Bad healing system
- Bad enemy placements 

Here is a list of the games positives: 
- Good build variety 
- Fun weapons 
- Good quests 
- Majula (one of the best hubs) 
- Fun DLC 
- Bonfire ascetics (refight bosses in ng+) 
- Best side quest content (ex. Darklurker) 
- Powerstancing 

My favorite bosses were definitely: 
- Darklurker 
- Fume knight 
- Burnt Ivory King 
- Sir Alonne 
- Smelter Demons 

In summary, the game is very punishing and annoying in certain systems, it has a ton of flaws, but it has a ton of content and I would recommend the game, especially for those who have already played souls or souls-like games.

After the completion of DS1, Miyazaki set his gaze on working for Sony. An exclusive game called Bloodborne. leaving a different team to work on a sequel. They were tasked with creating a new engine from scratch, with little guidance and troubled development they delivered a great game, controversial to some, a worthy successor for many. 

The review will be divided into three sections, and focusing specifically on if you should or not play the game, assuming you’re already a veteran of the series and know what makes these games great.

[b]Note: I’ll be omitting any SOFT improvement.[/b]

[b]A strongly-worded sentence:[/b] The average FromSoftware gamer sadly became amongst the most toxic communities, with acts of elitism or simply being one of Miyazaki’s lemmings, that can’t play the game for more than five minutes, because he’s not present to sprinkle fairy dust and some icing, If you’re one of those, then you should automatically avoid the game, chances are you’ll not like it, no matter how hard you try.

[h1][b]The bad:[/b][/h1] 

[b]Fall damage:[/b] Extremely punitive, feeling at times broken, even if you equip the cat ring. A limiting factor for certain exploration or experimentation.

[b]Adaptability:[/b] An I-frame tied stat, which pushes you into having to change the way you envision your builds.

[b]Hitboxes:[/b] Possibly the biggest problem with the game, you’ll be grabbed or hit by enemies even when you are not within their reach, same will work the other way around. Explosions also suffer from this issue, leaving to some gotcha moments. Backstabbing becomes a problem when the hitboxes are this crippled.

[b]Pathfinding:[/b] The AI at times will be lost, scurrying around, unceasingly, without a clear path, unable to reach you, leading to some lukewarm moments of hilarious laughter or frustration.

[b]Props and landscapes are botched:[/b] From very gorgeous areas, to scenery that feels stitched together in an amateurish way, the game also suffers from the lack of props to tell a story, making the world feel less empty.

[b]Audio glitches:[/b] An example would be during boss fights, when you hit them.

[b]Cutscenes:[/b] They tried adding cinematic black bars, it looks out of place, their attempt failed miserably.

[b]Curses:[/b] They feel pointless and inconsequential, at most giving you the same effect as a normal death, pop an effigy and you’re good to go. 

[b]Repetition of certain bosses:[/b] Recycling content isn’t new, but they could’ve toned it down a lil’. Couple of re-used bosses, even from the previous game.

[b]Map cohesion:[/b] DS1’s world was cohesive, connecting various paths and providing well-thought-out shortcuts for strategic bonfires. DS2 allows you to fast travel from the start, not much thought was put into how areas transition and connect, leading to vexing sights. Strategically placed bonfires would however gracefully return with shortcuts for the dlcs.

[b]Acid and the repair system:[/b] They're botched, your weapons will usually break far faster than you’d like, and to further complicate things, some areas or even enemies capitalise on that and punish you and especially your gear, leaving you frail and vulnerable. 

[b]Movement:[/b] Not as fluid as previous titles, a snap-in feel that might lead to accidental falls from a ledge when you try to quickly manoeuvre.

[b]Camera lock on:[/b] Never has been a forte of the souls series but somehow and in an unexplainable way the camera lock on feature feels even less responsive than it previously was.

[h1][b]The controversial:[/b][/h1]

[b]Human effigies:[/b] Few and scarce, extremely punitive unless you’re a veteran of the series and know when to use and not overuse them, one ring nullifies half of the effect.

[b]Life gems:[/b] DS1 nailed the healing system, focusing on a more fair and curated difficulty, being able to use one of your consumable items to increase the amount of flasks if you felt the need, 

DS2 tried something new, you’re given less flasks at the start, you’ll have to find them through the game, requiring you to use life gems, which are a one use consumable item, that you can simply buy infinite stacks of them at a vendor. 

[b]Bonfire Ascetic and enemies de-spawning:[/b] They allow you to turn an isolated area into a ng+ zone, resetting the enemies, bosses and items. Allowing you to farm de-spawning enemies again.

[b]Pharo lockstones and fragrant branches of yore:[/b] Pharo lockstones are an interesting addition, giving you some meaningful choices with what paths and rewards you choose, the problem is that fragrant branches  of yore do the same, defeating the purpose already.

[b]Torch mechanics:[/b] DS2 had big plans that shattered with a graphical downgrade, sadly torches were a casualty of that, they tried to salvage them, but usually you don’t really need them, so you can keep your shield for the most part. 

[b]Quantity over quality and certain backstabs:[/b] This point is extremely controversial, after the release of two Souls titles, veterans were storming through games, DS2 tried to spice things by making enemies harder and overwhelming in numbers, which led to the game feeling unfair and frustrating for some. They tried to counter a big issue with previous games where you circle around most enemies, and backstab them. One example of that are the turtle stone enemies, that counter backstabs.

[b]Nexus maiden:[/b] With a bit of Demon souls DNA, the maiden idea was brought back in DS2 and 3. Forcing us to move back and forth, back to the central hub, shoving fast travel down our throats, instead of just letting the player cater their basic levelling needs and move on, interrupted.

[b]GUI improvements:[/b] In some ways they did and in some they botched it, two examples would be how you consume multiple items and how much harder is to consult a weapon’s scale stat.

[h1][b]The good:[/b][/h1]

[b]Equipment variety and PVP:[/b] Fans will be spoiled with a massive amount of gear, truly giving us infinite replay value, especially with the glorious addition of powerstancing. PVP benefited greatly from this, which makes you wonder, why people hate on this game, yet it has the best PVP of the series, surely then the combat isn’t that bad is it? 

[b]Covenants and npcs:[/b] Npcs although a bit one dimensional compared to DS1, they feel interesting, they have their own intricacies a good amount of lore to share that spices the world.

[b]Decent amount of content and NG+:[/b] The game features a massive amount of content, NG+ isn’t lazily assembled, it has some new enemy types, new changes. DLCs are probably the best the series can offer, with interconnecting maps and less but more strategically placed bonfires, in some cases, even bringing puzzle and switch mechanics, if the base game had the dlc’s direction, it’d be the best DS game of the series, by far.

[h1][b]Last thoughts:[/b][/h1]
Demon souls possibly inspired by a great mix of many ideas seen in older games, like Legacy of Kain soul reaver or Onimusha, spawned its own genre, DS2 although flawed, delivered on that promise, the game is highly controversial but undeniably great and deserves in my opinion a strong 8.5 out of 10.

I have been playing an insane amount of Dark Souls over the past 2-3 months and wanted to offer my thoughts on the series as a whole. I played all of them on PC, back to back: DS3 with all DLCs (595 hours); DS2 SOTFS with DLCs (448 hours); and DS Remastered (148 hours), in that order. I got 100% completion (The Dark Soul) in all three. Yeah, that means I used a lot of online guides and robbed myself of the mystery. Done over, I'd forget the achievements until a third or fourth attempt.

Bottom Line up Front: I thoroughly enjoyed them all and can't choose a most or least favorite. Each is its own piece of art, but I can entirely sympathize with anyone who played them in their proper order, contemporaneous with their release, and found DS2 and DS3 derivative and not as ground breaking. Sure, but for anyone who does not have the emotional freight that comes with early adoption of a masterpiece series, they're all great games still worth playing today.

Gripes: DS3 is full of hackers, so I played mostly offline, only logging on for some tough boss fights once I'd maxed out all the PVP covenants. I imagine they all had a lot of hackers in their day, but DS3 is toxic at times. There's also a lot of great community out there and most player summons are helpful. Even most invaders are polite. DS2 SOTFS is not really PC/Keyboard/Mouse friendly. You have to disable double clicking every time. If you forget, you're dead in your first fight many times. That said, if you remap your keys and remember to disable double clicking, it's fine. There are quite a few hackers in SOTFS too, so many that I gave up on the arenas very quickly. Outside of the arenas, it's better at this point from a hacker perspective than DS3. DS Remastered was a gem. Even though it was my last DS game played, it was really cool seeing for myself what people meant when they said one or another aspect of the later games were homages to earlier ones. If I had any gripe it would be that subsequent playthroughs don't give you better ring versions, etc. That was one reason I kept at DS3 for so long. Getting the better stuff was fun and it was nice seeing new loot areas in the NG+ and NG++ rounds. This is not a major gripe at all -- i personally might have gone further in NG ++ with new or improved loot.

I highly recommend all three games and will post a copy of this on all three pages. Enjoy!

The black sheep of the entire series, Dark Souls II is the sequel to the critically acclaimed Dark Souls I and as you might expect, it didn't satisfy all of the fanboys when it came out. 

You might have played 1 or 3 and haven't bothered even touching 2 because of all the bad things that have been said about it by the community, reacting to it like the game murdered their families and stole their cupcakes. With all of that being said, just play the damn thing anyway. It may not be the best Souls game but it's still a great game and gives you a sense of adventure, and most of the hate just come from vitriolic Miyazaki fanboys that can't adjust to a different way of playing. 

Now I will elaborate on why you should still play this game, and keep in mind, this game is not perfect (just like any other Souls game). The combat is expanded on greatly from Dark Souls 1 and allows for much more customization. Power stancing, a wider range of hexes and spells, unique weapons that call upon cool effects and status buffs, expanded item list to accommodate for many playstyles are some of the many things that help with creating your own unique build and playstyle in this game. Even if you feel like you screwed up your build, DS2 introduced the ability to respec your character with a fairly common item. 

Another reason to play: the covenants and online activities actually work, they're not broken and buggy like in the first game. You want to PVP constantly? There's a covenant for that. You want to help others through the level by fending off invaders? There's a covenant for that.  Want to be a TMNT member and defend Master Splinter's rat cave? There's a covenant for that (no, really) You want to defend bells from the tall man that oppresses the midget overlords? There's a covenant for that. (No, I'm not high) You want to praise the sun with your brethren? Of course there's a covenant for that. Want to rub sandpaper on your crotch and make the game harder than it needs to be? First, you need a therapist. Second, there's a covenant for that!

I could go on and on about the good qualities like the length of the campaign being longer than 1 and 3 or the levels of fashion souls on display being unbelievable, but this is when I tell you of the bad aspects of the game. Keep in mind though, that these aren't deal breakers but they are annoying to most. 

The level design sucks for most of the game. Bonfire placement has been increased dramatically for the sake of the developers not knowing how to make the level connect as well as it did in 1 or 3. The tension of exploration doesn't really exist since you're likely to trip over another bonfire after straying away from your original one for 5 minutes. 

Most of the bosses aren't great; in fact some just feel like they were thrown in to fill out a quota. Prowling Magus, Najka, Twin Dragonriders, Covetous Demon etc etc. There are some good ones though and once you get to the DLC, they can even be awesome. 

While the lore is very interesting, some of the smaller tales feel unfinished.  Also don't get your hopes up for any of the loose threads to reach any resolution in DS3. The lore of that game almost pretends that Drangleic didn't even exist. 

So there are a million other things I could nitpick or praise, but that would take way too long. All in all, ignore the negative nitwits and just try the game for yourself, you might actually like it. It takes things from DS1 and expands upon them for gameplay and lore without ripping off characters and inserting them for nostalgia value. 

It's not like DS3 where it's on its knees with an open mouth, looking for DS1 senpai's approval the entire time.

First of all, Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin is an amazing game. No, it's not bad by any means, but certainly is the most controversial.

THE 5 MAJOR COMPLAINTS OF DS2
For the course of time, you'll hear things like "DS2 is the worst souls game", "ADP is garbage", Enemy placement is ridiculous", "The story is not good", "The bosses are bad", "Human Effigy is a bad game mechanic" and so on and so on. NOW, I will tell you all the truth. No bias, no rumors and no hate. Only what I experienced throughout my journey in this game:

1-ADP is garbage: The ADP (adaptability) is an exclusive stat only present in DS2. It is tied to your character's agility, which means it increases your I-frames (invincibility frames) when you dodge and roll. It's crucial that you spend some points here because otherwise you'll get hit hard and die a lot even if your character clearly rolled out of the way. And yeah, I can see why people were upset about this, because it can be an inconvenience, however, I don't mind. Yes, I like ADP. Mainly because it adds so much to your overall experience building your character. It doesn't take a lot to reach the Soft Cap, so all in all, it's alright. 

2-Enemy placement is ridiculous: Absolutely! I got jumped and ganked  so many times and it's annoying. Hordes of enemies will spawn out of thin air just so you have no escape. Iron Keep is one of the worst areas in this case. But come on, you know why this happens? Yeah, because you're rushing the area and trust me, this will not work. 3-The Story is not good: Not at all. The story is great and deeply interesting. I loved the NPCs in this game. I loved how much the environment tells a story. DS2 story is more "intimate". The bearer of the curse is one the best protagonists in the souls series and the journey through Drangleic is unforgettable. If you want to watch VaatiVidya lore videos, just do it. You'll appreciate it more with the context which you missed.

4-The bosses are bad: Yes, gameplay wise, they are. I mean, most of them are. Thing is, they're not as memorable as DS1 bosses nor are they like the spectacular DS3 bosses. Not even close. But eventually you'll learn to appreciate them in their own right. I can count 4 or 5 bosses that were genuinely good. But that's my opinion.

5- Human Effigy is a bad game mechanic: No, it's not. By the middle and certainly at the end of the game, you'll have a lot of human effigies, so they don't become a problem anymore. Also, it's one of the most important items in this game for lore and gameplay reasons. Period.

These are the 5 criticisms of DS2 that I heard the most. So I thought I could share my perspective about them. 

DS2 IS UNIQUE:
That's the main reason this game clicked with me so hard from the very beginning. DS2 has so many exclusive mechanics such as power stance, ADP and Bonfire Ascetic to name a few. Also the attention to detail in this game is off the charts! It uses a different engine from DS1 and 3, and personally I love it. The game is beautiful. Yes! Just arriving in Majula is something special. I cannot describe my admiration for all the Armours, weapons, places, vistas, covenants and music. In comparison to DS3, they're much more well made. Also, your character has way more personality in the way they move, their posture, their stance, their breathing. And you will not find this either in 1 nor 3, which is a shame. 

CONCLUSION:
Notice how I didn't share my thoughts about the "DS2 is the worst souls game" in the beginning? Well, I will say this here: It's not. DS2 is just way too different from what you've experienced in 1 and 3. And people can hate those differences or (in my case) love them, but these differences don't make the game bad. So, when you hear someone saying "Skip DS2. It's not worth it". Pay them no mind and play it for yourself. Give this one a chance and see if you'll enjoy it for what it is. I can assure you, everyone involved in its development poured a lot of love and dedication into it, even if this game passed through development hell and Miyazaki wasn't personally involved. Furthermore, always give it a try so you can draw your own opinion. Dark Souls 2 Scholar of the First Sin is not only the first Dark Souls game I did 100% but also is my favorite Dark Souls game. Yes, I love it and I totally recommend it. 

And always remember these words, Bearer of the curse: "Bear, seek, seek, lest".

Each Dark Souls game has notable strengths and weaknesses and this one is the most polarising by far. Some design choices were very innovative and clever while others were terrible.

Overall, it is my personal flawed favourite in the series.

Pros:
-Greatest viable build variety in the series.
-Best PvP in the series by far.
-Most interesting NPCs.
-Largest world.
-Largest number of different weapons and armours.
-Largest number of unique spells (sorc, faith, pyro, hex).
-Most balanced PvP (with one weird exception).
-Very atmospheric hub. My favourite in the FromSoft gaming universe.
-Greatest replayability (further NG+ cycles add unique enemies, different boss souls and drops).
-Bonfire ascetic mechanic pushes a single area into NG allowing you to refight bosses and experience the above benefits at a cost (enemies are much stronger).
-Most unique game in the series (recurring bosses, sconce lighting, traveling into memories, NPC who can be an invader or merchant depending on your choices etc).
-Really interesting covenants.
-Lots of NPC invasions with unique drops and behaviours.
-Widest variety of backstab and riposte animations by far.
-Best dual-wielding in the series.
-Many NPCs reward you meaningfully for spending lots of souls with them.
-Some armour items have stat boosts (cast speed, attunement slots, bleed bonus etc).
-You can respec an unlimited number of times, but requires a rare item that is tough to farm.
-Best dlc in the entire trilogy.

Mixed
-Including dlc, mostly better bosses than DS1 but worse than DS3.
-Fragrant branches and pharros lockstones are limited resources that you can use to unlock certain areas or NPCs. They are an interesting idea, but can be frustrating as they limit your choices.
-Enemies despawn after 12 kills but can be brought back by joining a covenant which also makes them stronger.
-In addition to estus, you get limited healing items that work over time.
-A common complaint is that this game often forces you into gank situations (multiple enemies attack you at once) which is difficult. However, I weirdly enjoy this as it forced me to learn how to deal with this (see bottom for tips).

Cons
-Worst player matching in the series by far. The soul memory mechanic matches you based on how much currency (souls) you have earned over your characters lifetime. This remains a disaster that requires you to sacrifice a ring slot for the Agape Ring that halts currency earning to sort-of counter. You can sacrifice another ring slot to help (Name Engraved Ring for a certain God makes players with the same God's ring match easier).
-Worst movement in the series, 8 directional lock. This is a major step back from DS1.
-Worst rolling and slowest healing. I-frames and healing item use speed depend on the AGL stat.
-Lots of enemies have grab attacks which are notorious for having overwhelmingly oversized hitboxes. While all grab attacks in every souls game are like this, DS2 has the highest number and most egregious offenders.
-One weapon is universally regarded as the best for PvP (thankfully it is not widely used in my experience).
-There is a baffling geographical choice that makes no sense, though I personally don't care.
-Like DS1 remastered, this version of the game split the playerbase from the original. However, the playerbase is very large and active mostly because of the excellent PvP.
__

PS. This is a really tough game, much harder than DS1 so I will include some tips:

-Shields
*Small-medium sized shields are excellent against small-human sized enemies but terrible against big enemies and bosses (you need to use greatshields or roll).

-Armour
*More useful for elemental resistance and stat bonuses (some pieces) than physical defence.

-Build
*Hard to go wrong! They did this better than any other DS game. Spell and Melee builds and hybrids are very viable. Generally bows and crossbows are support weapons though.

-Rolling and healing
*Level ADP to 26 to have a better time with rolling i-frames and healing faster.

-Multiple enemies
*When possible, use a ranged weapon or magic to draw one enemy at a time.
*Bait an enemy attack and run to seperate them up. Take the opportunity to wack them a few times and repeat.
*Use your environment to force enemies to chase you. During the run, they almost always separate. (ALWAYS RUN BACK, NEVER FORWARD unless you know it's safe). Again, Take the opportunity to wack them a few times and repeat.
*Ensure you have a weapon or spell that you can use safely (fast enough, won't get caught on environment) with length, sweep or aoe.

I hope you consider buying this and that you'll enjoy it as much or more than I have. Good luck!

[i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i] is such an insanely rich and expansive game; FromSoft could have released two separate games. Which is kind of what they did. 

Back when [i]Dark Souls II[/i] was first released people considered it a hollow and bleak follow up to the original [i]Dark Souls[/i], me included. However it wasn’t without its high points and strengths. FromSoft took much criticism to heart and released three DLC packs with an incredible amount of content in each to offset some of the lacklustre areas from the main game, as well adding several elements that pad up the lacking story somewhat. They wrapped it all up in a new graphics package, slapped a full price tag on it and flung it back onto the selves. A gutsy strategy, but the game is better for it. The game is an immersive role-playing monster that keeps sucking you in. Furthermore, it has an insane amount of options and content to explore and exploit. Finally, it retools and refines many of its predecessor’s aspects. [i]Dark Souls II[/i] is a behemoth of a game that merits any self-respecting gamer’s attention. 

[i]Dark Souls II[/i] picks up thousands of years after the original [i]Dark Souls[/i] and continuously throws you down a well of unyielding challenges and adversity with the express purpose of hardening you for the next battle. The original world of [i]Dark Souls[/i] is gone and in its place is a dilapidated, nearly abandoned kingdom called Drangleic. You are an undead, who ventures to this land to find a cure for your, and your family’s hollowing condition. The game sets of off with the bare minimum, as is a staple of the FromSoft narrative style. You’re forced to discover the bulk of the story for yourself. This is where the developers went overboard. Instead of hiding plot and infusing it with delicious lore, they now provide you with the bare minimum of plot and nearly drown you in lore. Admittedly, the lore of [i]Dark Souls II[/i] is incredible and novels could be written on its depth and enriching character. However, the lack of apparent plot rather withholds you from thoroughly exploring it. You, as the player, are not motivated to investigate items, characters, or world as explore. The only thing you’re told a few minutes in is to “seek the king”. When you eventually do find the man in question he’ll tell you to seek adversity. Finally facing the final boss is punctuated with a resounding “what the hell was that?” 
The thing is, that when you finally discard the narrative’s notions, and do explore on your own accord, you’ll be rewarded immensely. It seems almost as if FromSoft did not just want to make the gameplay difficult, but also the story. The Scholar of the First Sin edition provides some context to the ordeal, but you’re mostly left to your own devices in terms of plot direction and interpretation. 
While the story may not be too captivating, the general gameplay is thoroughly addictive. It is common knowledge at this point that the [i]Souls[/i] series are difficult. The difficulty spike from other games requires you to learn and to invest effort. The eventual successes after many a loss will feel monumental. This risk reward structure is enthralling to say the least. Not only do you earn valuable progress, but also experience and valuable items to customise your character and playstyle. 

[i]Dark Souls II[/i] is a genuinely personal experience, and the game offers you near countless tools to differentiate and customise your experience. While the game does force you to picks a class at the very beginning, you easily deviate from your initial resume. From the starting area the world lies open at your feet. Hundreds of weapons to try. Dozens of armours to wear. Loads of magic spells to learn. Zounds of monsters to slay. The game lends itself to all manners of play. You can play a buffed out tank and brave hordes in plate mail. Or stay lithe and swift and put out ludicrous amounts of damage. Physical matter not your thing? The try the magic arsenal. We have lighting, darkness, fire, and poison; even this blue stuff that just kills things. You can have it any way you want, and hardly any play through will be the same. There are even special weapons that combine the styles. The insane degree to which you can adjust, mix and match makes for some incredible fidelity. It is therefore good that the game also has a respec button to mulligan your build when you see fit. 
However, it is important that your stomping grounds for your personal build is well tilled, and unfortunately, that is not always the case in [i]Dark Souls II[/i]. While character tools are amazing, the level design is somewhat lacking. Rather washed-out areas and straight corridor stages make up the majority of world. A true shame, because the original [i]Dark Souls[/i] and its predecessor [i]Demons’ Souls[/i] all had environments that were maze like and harrowing to traverse. Making it to the short cut in the old games was a relief. In [i]Dark Souls II[/i] it’s just a convenience. This issue is mostly resolved in the three DLC areas that send you into completely disorienting maze like tombs, towers and cities to fight even deadlier enemies, but also find even more and better loot. 

From a technical standpoint, [i]Dark Souls II[/i] addresses many complaints from its predecessors, but also introduces some new, and unwelcome changes. Praise be to the sun when the backstab got nerfed. Praise be to Vendrick when the online connection now takes place via dedicated servers instead of P2P. Hail to the crowns for the new dual wield animations that allow for the amazing samurai, ninja and berserker builds that flay and destroy the many bosses. [i]Dark Souls II[/i] has taken care to make good on several sigmatic issues with the original, and FromSoft has succeeded in most cases. The result is a more playable and durable system that is more manageable to use. 
On the flipside though, the game introduces a stat called soul memory to govern the interaction between players. It basically changes the thresholds for cooperation and invasions from level based to purely experience based. This skews to balance to nearly ridiculous levels where proper online play becomes extremely hard or downright non-existent until you manage to reach a later section of the game where you may or may not fit in. Furthermore, boss design, the Souls’ series great pride, has taken a hit. Most bosses are souped up guys in armour with broken tracking and disjointed hitboxes. The number of monstrosities that do show up are hardly a challenge. Some fights against these blood knights are extremely amazing, but the majority is forgettable. Once again, the DLC bosses fix this issue to a great extent. 
In general, enemy design is based on “guys in armour.” What is even worse is that FromSoft decided to just go for the horde approach when it came to enemy placement and difficulty tweaks. When you die it’s either due to a horde of cheap, enemies, or one enemy with infallible tracking on its weapon. The Scholar version addresses this with amended enemy placement, but the damage is already done. 

Despite some shortcomings, the overwhelming amount of content, immersion and options ultimately make [i]Dark Souls II[/i] a main course on any video game dinner menu. The meaty length and beefy options allow for a multitude of approaches that can fit anyone’s playstyle. While the story doesn’t flavour the dish too much, the underlying textures provide a distinct taste that will have to dig in a little deeper. Although the chef’s final changes may divide the guests on what wine goes best with it, at the end of it, you’ll be satisfied and well fed.
