Compared to Dark Souls 1, this game is much more consistent in its quality, with lower highs but higher lows. There's nothing in DS2 that's awful on the level of Lost Izalith, but there's also nothing nearly as good as the Painted World outside of the DLC. However, with the DLC included for free in the SotFS edition, the game is elevated to much greater heights. Sinh, Fume Knight, and Ivory King are among the best bosses in all of Dark Souls, better than almost every fight from DS1 and a good chunk of the DS3 boss pool as well. They also contextualize the story of the game in a way that makes the game far more personal -- it's much easier to be invested in the world of DS2 compared to DS1 and 3 where the stories feel like a backdrop rather than motivation.

COMBAT
Combat is Dark Souls combat, I don't feel I need to explain much more than that. It lends itself more to larger groups of enemies, and magic is greatly improved, but it's still Dark Souls, and it's just as good as any other Dark Souls game -- faster than DS1 as your attack options are better, but slower than DS3 because multiple enemy encounters require patience and picking a good time to attack -- the Dual Pursuers in NG+ play more like Ornstein and Smough than as a generic combat encounter. PvP is also great, but my experience is too limited to comment on it in depth here.

PRESENTATION
The game is, unfortunately, ugly -- much less creative enemy designs than DS1 and 3, with most of the new enemies being fairly standard humanoid enemies or bland looking 'fantasy monster' -- Ogres, those weird mushroom things, and the long-armed green enemies in No Man's Wharf are all forgettable enemy designs, a far cry from the unique appearance of the basilisks, the unnatural bodies of the mimics, and the horrifying bug/human hybrids in the depths of Blighttown. Boss design suffers from a similar lack of quality -- there are no fights as visually striking as Sif, Gaping Dragon, or Gravelord Nito. The most creative boss design is the Executioner's Chariot, an optional boss that culminates in a fight against a pretty generic horse enemy with dodgy hitboxes.

LEVELS & BOSSES
Speaking of bosses, outside of the DLC the boss design in this game is downright bad. I can honestly say that there wasn't a single fight that impressed me in the entire base game. In stark contrast, the levels between these boss fights are fantastic, and with a couple exceptions they were all well designed. I didn't like Heide's Tower or Earthern Peak, and I still can't tell if Shrine of Amana is a great zone or an awful one, but every other zone felt satisfying to fight through and explore, with plenty of secrets to discover and interesting enemy set ups that forced me to adapt to a very steady difficulty curve throughout each 'path' -- the first zones, like Forest of Fallen Giants or Shaded Ruins, were generally pretty simple and straight forward, with some kind of mechanic the zone wanted to teach you, be it curse pots, poison build up, combat against large enemies, combat against many smaller enemies, etc., but each level path would iterate on these ideas, often culminating in a final stretch to the boss that is a grueling test in all of the lessons you've learned -- the cave before Freja, the flooded hallway before Sinner -- or in an optional but very difficult boss with an even more challenging run-up -- Smelter Demon, Belfry Gargoyles if you're online -- that makes the rest of the zone easier to tackle in some fashion.

WORLD
The most conflicting part of this game is whether or not I hate the gameworld or adore it. Dark Souls 1 had an amazingly interconnected world throughout the first half of the game, but threw this concept out the door in the second half besides a few cool moments, like seeing Izalith through a hole in the wall in Tomb of Giants. Dark Souls 3 didn't have many interconnected paths between zones, but instead focused on feeling more like a journey than a quest, moving through the world in a linear fashion with a tightly controlled difficulty curve. Dark Souls 2 has multiple paths that you can tackle in almost any order, allowing you to tackle the game the way you choose to -- and not in the "well, technically" fashion of Dark Souls 1, but by having a more consistently challenging game that retains its difficulty regardless of what path you go down. However, these paths do the infuriating and yet somewhat fascinating thing of refusing to make any logical sense. You walk through tunnels that teleport you from daylight in a forest to rainy nighttime on a mountain, you climb elevators that lead from the top of a tower upwards to the base of a volcano that doesn't even exist, and your tutorial zone is called Things Betwixt, as though its lodged between worlds in some way, and the only exit is through a crack in the barrier between the world of Drangleic and the world of Things Betwixt. If it wasn't a concept that was explored further in Dark Souls 3, culminating in the complete devolution of time and space in The Ringed City, it would be easy to call this lazy design, but its clear in retrospect that this game is very intentionally building an atmosphere of unreality that is utterly fascinating to look closely at once you start to pay attention to it and look at how many ways the game's story and world ties into this idea.

DLCS

Sunken King plays like a Zelda level, with a bow and arrow being necessary to explore the level. Most of the bonfires are hidden and well spaced, and I could see somebody getting through the whole DLC only ever finding two of them. Enemies are challenging to fight, and the ghostly suits of armour are a very interesting challenge that I won't spoil, even if I struggle to imagine being able to defeat them all on just one life. Sinh is the best endurance fight in the series, and possibly the best dragon fight in the series -- I'm still torn on whether or not Midir is the ultimate challenge or just obnoxious -- with his movements making him difficult to follow across the room and his damage being difficult to avoid. Taking him down feels like a triumph simply because the odds are so stacked against you, with the durability damaging armour plating, the toxic building flame he spits at you, and the massive hitboxes of many of his attacks.

Old Iron King has the best level design in any Dark Souls game ever, with an absolutely perfect understanding of how to pace the DLC. The DLC only has one mandatory boss fight, and he is an incredible challenge, and certainly the best humanoid boss pre-Dark Souls 3, where the humanoid boss bar was raised so high that nothing could ever reach it. When you activate the elevators that span the tower, what was previously an incredibly difficult to navigate maze becomes much more accessible, and dozens of secrets are opened to you. Incredibly satisfying level design elevates this DLC to the top of the pack.

Ivory King is the worst of the DLC, but has the perfect fight to end your DLC experience with, as Ivory King is the most gorgeously presented boss in the entire series. However, exploring the level twice after melting the ice feels tedious, and the Frigid Wastes are a war crime. Although great, I spent more time being lost than making progress in this DLC.

FINAL THOUGHTS
Overall, this game is a solid 8/10 for the base game, weighed down by poor boss encounters and bland presentation but carried by a top-notch combat and progression system, but a 9/10 once DLC is included, with the drought of good bosses being augmented with several fights ranging from great (Aava, Elana) to fantastic (Fume Knight, Sinh, Ivory King), the story being heavily improved, and the already great level designed being honed to perfection.

Dark Souls 2 is my favorite of the Dark Souls games.

Now hear me out here. Put away your torches and pitchforks. Yes you, in the front. I mean you. Put that torch out. Let me finish.

I know Dark Souls 2 is the red headed stepchild of the soulsborne series. A lot of people complain about the lack of speed in combat compared to DS3 or Bloodborne and they dislike the janky level design compared to the realistic flow between areas in DS1 and Demon's Souls. Dark Souls 2 however has plenty of things going for it that people just don't give it credit for.

For one, I'd say this one is probably THE MOST friendly of the games to newcomers. In Dark Souls 1 you've got the dreaded skeleton graveyard that straight up murders newbies, and there is a lot of annoying spots that will one shot people who aren't expecting to be burned by 
dragon fire on a bridge for example. Dark Souls 3 has the VERY fun experience for new players where the first boss they encounter will straight up murder them if they don't learn the game mechanics pretty quick.

Oh are you like my wife and aren't instantly good at a game upon picking it up? Maybe you need a few hours to work out the kinks? Well invest in spare controllers because the first and third games will make you smash them against some walls while you figure out what exactly you are doing wrong.

Dark Souls 2 however, has a rather gentle newbie area that teaches you exactly how the game works in a safe environment. It then offers you two choices of areas to explore that teach you the exact benefit of different mechanics after you arrive to majula, the main safe zone. You can go to the soldiers keep, which has a lot of hordes of quick enemies that will test your ability to block and fight groups. Or you can go the other route, which features a lot of slow moving big enemies that test your ability to judge distances of attacks and dodge.

It also features a dragon rider that doesn't ride his dragon. Not that I'm complaining, I'm just saying he doesn't live up to his name.

These two areas are genius as far as game design. They allow the player to build up skills in a relatively safe environment and become better at the game. They teach you, unknowingly, the foundational skills that will help you progress through the rest of the game. They also drop some pretty good gear early on that can serve you up till midway through the game with some decent weapon variety.

This is how I learned to Dark Souls. You know that whole "git gud" thing.

See I started, like many other people, in DS1. I played several hours and got brutally murdered by skeletons. Then I came back a week later and made it all the way to the demon ruins with nothing but wander's garb and a +1 Falchion. Which I feel is an achievement in and of itself.

Don't downplay my achievements. I deserve my participation medal just like all the other kids.

Yet I kept getting murdered trying to climb back out. Every time I tried to leave up through the swamps I'd find myself dying. I couldn't escape the area, I didn't know how to get better, and this was when the game first came out so I didn't have a wiki to tell me what to do otherwise. I finally gave up in disgust. It was just so frustrating and confusing.

A few years later, DS2 comes out and I pick it up on a whim if nothing else. What I found was a completely different experience. Dark Souls 2 can not be praised enough for its incredibly teachable game design. Enemies are introduced slowly over the course of the game. Optional areas are plentiful to give you a reason to go back and explore when you get the right items to seek them out. Items are doled out carefully over the time you play so as not to overwhelm you with a bewildering amount of items (Like Dark Souls 1 often would) or give you amazing items late in the game after you'd already picked and upgraded the weapon you liked (Like Dark Souls 3 did).

Looking at you Sunlight Straight Sword.

This gave me the chance to really understand exactly how to play the game. I learned how to parry. I learned how to circle strafe bigger enemies. I learned how to judge distances and become better at dodging.

Basically, I stopped sucking at Dark Souls. Not at life though, it didn't help me with that. I still use my Dark Souls skills as a band aid for my failures as a person.

I might be in debt but I can beat The Nameless King without taking a hit. So there is that.

My point is, that this is a game that is great at teaching you how to play it and what the rules are. The bosses are fun and never overbearing, and I never felt at a single time in this game that I died due to some stupid unfair BS like a dragon burning me alive as I crossed a bridge. Every death felt earned, like *I* had made the mistake. It never beat me over the head with a hammer and left me in a ditch like Dark Souls 1 did.

I still can't walk down the hardware isle at Walmart.

Overall Dark Souls 2 is just really fun. It slowly ramps up the difficulty in a way that is fair and the NPC encounters in this one I find to be really compelling. I sought out Lucatiel of Mirrah every chance I could because I wanted to know what became of her. I followed the rivalry between Creighton and Pate and chose who to side with in the end. (I chose against Pate, because screw that guy) I sought out all the knights to fight alongside me against the burned Ivory King so I could lay him to rest. Point being, I was invested. There's some damn good NPC quests in this one, more so that in later or earlier installments. It was a bit odd for a Dark Souls game, but its probably one of the reasons why I like it so much.

Yes I know, Dark Souls 2 breaks the mold and I like it. Stop the presses. No seriously stop them, I thought I saw a human finger back there.

The DLCs for Dark Souls 2 are also in my opinion, the best DLCs in a Dark Souls game to date. I mean, don't get me wrong, I love The Ringed City in Dark Souls 3. But fighting Sir Alonne in Dark Souls 2 was an absolute joyful challenge that I look forward to every time I do a new run through the game. The aformentioned Ivory King battle is also a fun and also emotionally charged fight that geniunely makes you feel sorry for this cursed great king that you have to put down.

Dark Souls 2 isn’t Dark Souls 1. It shares a lot of the broader strokes and some things that are basically unchanged, even down to its name and story, but it differs in the finer details, which is what matters if you are expecting to find more Dark Souls. And while Dark Souls 2 is different, the majority of the changes made vastly improved upon the gameplay, while the storytelling and world cohesion suffered. Dark Souls 2 is also a lot bigger than Dark Souls 1, though a huge amount of the content is optional. This means the experience isn’t as tight and focused as Dark Souls 1 (well, as the first half of Dark Souls 1), but on the other hand, it’s a lot more replayable (as if my playtime didn’t already clue you in on that). Now, since Steam limits reviews to 8000 characters, I can only write the rest of my opinions in the form of bullet-points, so if you want a more fleshed out version of this review with pretty graphics, here is a link for you:
[url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0M1oq-Ti60I&feature=youtu.be]Dark Souls 2 review and critique[/url]

Otherwise…

Pros:
[list]
[*]There’s a power stance mechanic that allows you to use 2 weapons at once. It gets kind of complicated, and isn’t explained at all in-game, so looking it up might be a good idea. There’s tons of stuff to experiment with, so I highly recommend checking it out.
[*]The upgrade paths from Dark Souls 1 makes a return in the form of the infusion system, though it functions somewhat differently. Rather than spending a ton of unique materials to make a +5 Chaos Zweihander or whatever, essentially locking down your options to 1 or 2 paths, In Dark Souls 2 you instead upgrade your weapon (or shield) normally while having the option at any point to infuse or un-infuse without losing your upgrades. Some options have been removed, 2 have been changed and 4 new options have been introduced. One of the options being…
[*]Dark! Yes, that is implemented into the base game this time, and Dark damage now scales with the lowest of your Faith and Intelligence. Hexes are their own type of spell, and are unique in that they require both Intelligence and Faith to cast.
[*]The game looks good. Like, really, really good. Possibly the best looking game I’ve played, honestly.
[*]The character-creation is extremely flexible, and if you spend enough time with it, you can pretty much create anything you want.
[*]Durability has drastically been reduced, but it also resets at bonfires. This means the durability is a real factor when judging whether or not a weapon is viable for PvE or PvP, unlike in Dark Souls 1 where repairs was something done willy-nilly.
[*]PvP. Dark Souls 2 supposedly the best PvP in the trilogy (I haven’t tried Dark Souls 3 (yet), but it’s certainly a lot better than in Dark Souls 1). Nearly every half-decent build is viable, and invading in the DLC areas is some of the most fun I’ve had with the game.
[*]Really damn good DLCs. No Artorias of the Abyss, but, not too far from it either. Plenty of fun items can be found (like the Bone Fist; <3 the Bone Fist).
[/list]

Cons:
[list]
[*]The hollowing mechanic. Every time you die (or get cursed), you lose 5 % maximum health until you reach 50 % health. This usually ends in a destructive spiral that only punishes inexperienced players. There is however a ring you can get that reduces the penalty somewhat, so that might be worth looking into if you get stuck.
[*]Dwindling multiplayer. There’s many reasons for this (split versions of Dark Souls 2 (make sure you buy the right version for your system), the fact that Dark Souls 3 is out, no cross-platform support etc.), so if you’re considering buying this, I would recommend buying it ASAP.
[*]The adaptability stat. Remember the resistance stat from Dark Souls 1? Well, they crowbarred it into this game as well, but your invincibility frames while rolling is also tied to it. Which means your rolls early on does fuck-all to prevent damage.
[*]Impressively bad hitboxes, which makes the adaptability stat an even worse idea, since rolling pretty much becomes mandatory. Thought you were out of range of the hippogre grab attack? Think again, fool! *chomp, chomp, ded*.
[*]Enemies tend to aggro in groups, so your environmental puzzle-solving skills from Dark Souls 1 will do very little to help as a conga-line of enemies queue up to bring you down.
[*]The writing is a lot worse, in that it’s lost all its subtlety and is just plain bad. There’s one character who says “he sorts of looks like my father. He’s a blacksmith too, you see” before dismissing the idea; dude literally sits within earshot of the conversation, but nope, never bothers to check.
[*]Soul Memory. I personally wasn’t too affected by this, since I usually pump all my souls into levels anyway, but if you like to PvP or Co-op, this might be an issue for you. There is a ring that eats all your souls so your Soul Memory stays the same, but on the other hand, [i]it eats all your souls[/i].
[/list]

Well I finally got around to finishing Dark Souls 2, and I have to say I have slightly mixed feeling about it. For those of you who don't know much about the development, the dark souls franchise was created by Hitataki Miyazaki, who was the director of the PS3 exclusive Demon's Souls, and then its spiritual successor Dark Souls 1, and then later went on to direct Bloodborn and Dark Souls 3, but due to the development of Dark Souls 2 and Bloodborn overlapping, he was unable to direct Dark Souls 2, making it the only game in the souls-born "franchise" to not of had him as its lead, and it definitely shows. I would easily say this is the worst of the 3 dark souls games, but thats not saying its a bad game, just not as good as the other two games which I would consider masterpieces. There are many great things about this game, but also many no so great things, but I will go over them below in more detail. You will find I compare this game alot to DS3, and this is because I think DS3 is the game that most people that have played a DS game will have played, and it is also the DS game that I have played the most, by far, so I can easily draw comparisons to it.

First, the pros:

- Its a Dark Souls game. This might sound stupid, but there is something special about the concept of a DS game. From having your ass kicked time after time, the fear of dying due to losing your souls upon death, the anticipation of where the next bonfire will be, and whether or not you should keep going, and risk losing your souls, or turn back, when the next bonfire could be right around the corner. The immense feeling of satisfaction when a boss you have been stuck on for hours is finally slain. All these things are some of the many defining aspects of a souls game, and they are all present here, which I think is worthy of me pointing out.

- DS2 is a beautiful game. The locations, for the most part, look good, if not stunning, and there is far more variety both in terms of geometry and colour usage compared to DS3. Where DS3 felt rather bland and dead, and most areas were either grey or brown and rather desaturated, DS2 is quite bright and colourful in some areas, and as someone who went from playing DS3 to DS2 the more varied enviroments and usage of colour is a nice change.

- The game has good enemy variety to go along with these areas. As I approached the end of DS3, I felt like I had met most of the enemies before, and the challenge had started to ware off abit as enemies were mostly predictable, and I already knew their weaknesses and strengths. But in DS2, there feels to be a much wider variety of enemies making the combat more varied and more challenging, IMO. The enemies are not just varied in thier looks and weapons, but also in their attacks, and how they behave.

Now, the cons:

- Sadly, the combat in this game just feels very clunky and not very consistent. I wasn't expecting it to feel as fluid as DS3, as its not running in the newer engine that DS3 does, but everything just feels like a downgrade over DS1. The rolling feels static and to slow, invincibility frames are almost non existant, you take damage while opening chests, performing backstabs, going through fog walls. There just seems to be alot of stupid design decisions to try to make the game "harder", but not necessary in a fair way, and this does not just apply to the combat, but I will go into this more later. I don't think it is fair for you to take damage while you are trapped in an animation that you cannot end, which is exactly why both DS1 and 3 gave you invicibilty while performing certain actions, but this seems to have been massively scaled back in this game, and there is no good reason as to why. Alot of the weapons also feel very "samey" to me, like there is not as much variety as I would of liked, but this is a very personally complaint that not everyone will have an issue with. There is also a bug with weapon durability that causes weapons to break twice as fast when playing the game at 60fps, which is very annoying, and still is not fixed to this day.

- This probably should go under combat, but it is such a big issue for me I am giving it its own section. So what am I talking about? The hitboxes. One of the key features of a souls game over many other challenging game, is their fairness. When you die in DS, 99.9% of the time it is because you screwed up, and has nothing to do with the game. But in DS2 this is not true at all. I have died countless times in this game, due to enemies hitting me when I should of been out of reach, their weapons have clipped through walls and knocked me of a ledge, their spells have traveled through the surroundings and hit me when I thought I was safe. This just becomes very infuriating, because while DS1 and 3 are not perfect, and have their own issues, the enemy hit boxes are nowhere near as buggy and inconsistent as they are in this game, which leads me to believe that this game was rushed out early, before the combat was fully polished, probably to make room for the release of bloodborn the following year, but this is pure speculation.

- Enemy placement is another key part of the souls games that seems to have been changed just for the sake of making the game harder. Alot of the time you will just find yourself getting outnumbered in this game, which can be very infuriating when you have 5 or 6 guys all attacking at the same time, and your stamina gets drained instantly and there is nothing you can do but sit back and die. I havn't played the original version of DS2 yet, but from what I have been told, the changes made to enemy placement in DS2:SotFS actually made things worse, and not better.

- One of the biggest disappointments in this game is the boss design. The main attraction of the DS games, for many people, including myself, is the bosses. But sadly, this game seems to hold most of the worst bosses in the souls-born series. Im not saying they are all bad, and there are plently of good ones, but this game goes for quantity over quality. For example, DS1 has a total of 22 bosses, DS3 has 19, but DS2 has 32 bosses, excluding DLC. There are atleast 2 bosses in this game that are a pure copy and paste from DS1, and some others that are just a group of normal enemies they decided to stick behind a fog wall and call a boss. There are some very good ones, but alot of very terrible ones, and the issues with the combat and rolling that I listed above don't help things. There are also quite alot of gank bosses, where, again, they have just decided to throw you in against multiple enemies to make the game harder, but not more fun.

- The final major issue I have with this game is the healing. DS2 added an item called a life gem, that allows you to have an additional heal outside of your estus flask. The only problem is the entire system doesn't feel balanced at all. You can carry up to 99 life gems on you at a time, and they are sold at a very cheap price of only 300 souls each, and an unlimited quantity making the game very easy to cheese in some areas. I think they could of made the healing much better overall, firstly by limiting the number of life gems you can carry to around 20 so they are not quite so over powered. I also think you should be able to move while using estus, like in DS3, because you can move while using life gems, which kind of makes the estus flask obsolete when you can just pop a couple of life gems which will do the exact same job, just slightly slower but with more manoeuvrability.

The conclusion: 
Judging by how much of this review was spent talking about the negatives, you are probably thinking that I must have hated this game, but I didn't. I would say it was a little disappointing, but it is still a DS game, and still alot of fun, but it does have its issues. Overall, I would say that I recommend DS2 because while its not as good as the other 2 games in many peoples opinions, its still alot of fun to play, despite the issues.

Let's start by the game itself, Dark Souls II. A solid entry to the world of Dark Souls, it takes on what Dark Souls left behind and made a whole new world and lore upon it. The game IS related to the original Dark Souls, but it tries to be a thing of it's own at the same time by creating pretty much a whole new plot in the game. You're no longer seeking the flame, you're not trying to keep the age of fire going (or trying to kill it), you're trying to save yourself for a curse, a curse that no known man has managed to steer clear off.

The lore of this game is definitely solid, and you'll quickly realize about it as soon as you progress a little bit and pay attention to your surroundings, NPCs and certain items.

Now, gameplay-wise, this game is a lot more "neutral" towards playstyles. You're not constantly forced to be overly agressive as in the latter Dark Souls 3, nor are you considerably stronger by becoming a poise monster. Dark Souls II manages a pretty neat balance between builds, both with and against you. You'll find yourself pretty comfortable changing playstyles and builds since MOST of them will remain as viable as the rest (Granted pure INT builds are insane in PvE, and pure FTH builds are dogshit in PvE).

The game definitely isn't flawless, but it more than makes up for it's mistakes with many aspects of the game itself. It's surprisingly long, but it never feels "too long", you'll keep progressing awaiting the next area with it's new location and set of enemies (Ironically the game was supposed to be much larger and as interconnected as DS1, but... Strict development times did their magic along with direction issues, so this is what we ended up with).

All in all, Dark Souls II is definitely a GREAT game, it's a great entry to it's series, and to it's genre as a whole. Don't let the usual mockery around the game fool you, there's a lot more to this game than the jokes and memes will show you.

Just... Don't go into this game expecting a fast-paced action game, cause it's far from that.

Dark Souls II is many things its siblings are not. 

It is the only from software game where your left hand weapon has a full moveset; completely ambidextrous. 
It's the only fromsoft game where you can infuse almost any weapon, and buff infused weapons. 
It's the only one where you can dual wield weapons of different classes. 
It's the only one where you can strap two bones to your fist and do a hadouken. 
It's the only one where you can buff a chime with lightning from another chime, making that first chime deal more damage with lightning spells. 
It's the only one with not one but TWO shields that cast miracles (one which casts hexes), A mace that casts hexes and miracles, a sword, twinblade, and a spear that cast sorcery, and a shield that is a crossbow.

Buildcraft in this game is unmatched. The developers clearly had player creativity in mind, and removed as many limitations as possible which were seen in prior (and succeeding) fromsoft games. There is very little restriction on what you can and cannot do with your weapons and equipment, and it leads to a tremendously deep experience when planning builds and experimenting with playstyles. There's really nothing else like it; not even Elden Ring boasts the same diversity of tactics.

BTW don't listen to what people tell you; you don't have to level ADP, at least not so much. DS2's bosses and enemies are designed less around being dodge rolled through, and more around finding the blind spots and gaps in attacks, and using good footwork to strafe around them. 

Rolling is more committal in this game, and rolling attacks go in the direction you rolled, which leaves you with much shorter openings where you have to re-orient after a dodge before you can strike. But if you can master walking just at the edge of swings, placing yourself in their blind spots, and pushing in at the right time to retaliate while they're committed to their own attacks, you may never have to dodge at all. In that sense, rolling should be seen as a last-resort when your positioning is bad, not the modus operandi. Personally I find this game much more satisfying, and the boss fights much elevated, when trying to dodge as little as possible, rather than dodging everything like I would in DS3 or ER.

It's also a game that clearly wants you to play co-operatively. Dark Souls 1 was a game where it was extremely easy to run past almost every challenge the game had, once you learned the layout and enemy aggro ranges a bit. There was little incentive to summon players for anything other than a boss you were stuck on. In DS2, the level design is evidently more punishing to solo players, and sometimes even a bit mean; but with a friend, these challenges are perfectly manageable, and clearly summoning was the intented method of play for a lot of locations. 

You can still play solo if you want to, but it demands a degree of patience. You have to be willing to take things slow, bait out enemies individually, or commit to using equipment that's good at dealing with groups. You can't expect to move around freely everywhere you go, or run past enemies without concern. Nothing in this game is genuinely unfair, so long as you exercise patience and presence of mind. Keep an eye and ear out, take caution when entering new areas, be ready to back up and always have a place in mind to back up to. 

Most importantly, have fun with it; it's not a big deal if you die, and often you'll die in ways that really should be funny. This game has an exceptional sense of humor, there are so many cheeky details and silly traps that the developers clearly had a blast designing. Let it be funny to you, stop taking to your keyboard to malign every "unfair" death, odds are you're not doing a no-hit challenge run.

Dark Souls II is a magnificent yet flawed work of art that only gained its unjustified infamy due to not being able to top its predecessor (and possibly successor) in terms of consistent quality, especially from a gameplay perspective. it's not necessarily a harder game than Dark Souls I, but it certainly feels a lot more unforgiving, ruthless, and exasperating just for the sake of provoking the player at times, especially in the early game and the DLCs. 

I could list a bunch of questionable changes that can turn off a lot of players, but I find it hypocritical for most people to whine about this game when the first game also had its fair share of moments that could give any sane person violent tendencies. in my opinion, criticizing areas and bosses based on their difficulty and how fun they are in these games is pointless because they have many variables such as play style and character build and sometimes even luck - it's all subjective. despite this, what makes "ds2 sucks just skip it" an invalid opinion in most cases is the fact that one important thing Dark Souls I teaches you is to be patient, and as long as you play Dark Souls II patiently there is nothing intolerable about this game, and you'll see that most of the "issues" people list about this game are non-issues that merely leave you frustrated until you manage to finish the area and then you're left with that sweet feeling of satisfaction again. not to mention there is an odd stigma around this game where people just decide that this game is bad even without playing it themselves. for me, the only tedious part of this game was it had a lot of repetition, especially with the bosses, but for the most part, I've had a lot of fun playing it. that's why I believe this game is definitely a must play for anyone who is getting into Dark Souls. 

what makes Dark Souls II special for me is that it does not try to replicate what Dark Souls I did. instead, it focuses on the fundamentals of Dark Souls I on a much smaller scale, allowing the narrative to explore some untouched parts of the lore in more detail. in Dark Souls I, you're a significant part of a grand creation tale, tasked with deciding the fate of this world, and meeting all the legends behind its origin during your adventure. in Dark Souls II, however, you're in one of the many kingdoms of an already broken and hopeless world. all over Drangleic, you see the aftermath of the grand events of Dark Souls I and prior. your mission is still breaking the curse, but this time, you're rarely encouraged by anyone to play your part and do the "right" thing. instead, you're persistently encouraged to question. question the cycle, question the conceited ideas planted in your head by others, question yourself, and question the rest of the world. you're asked again and again, what do YOU want to do? after all is done, do you have the courage to take a step towards the unknown - beyond the light and the Dark? 

despite being widely different from it, this game truly carries the soul of Dark Souls I and it will give you just as much to contemplate once you're done. for this reason I highly recommend Dark Souls II.

Late to the party for Dark Souls 2 also, and the general anthem I'd been hearing about it is general negativity from the community. So maybe it's because I went in with those sorts of expectations, but overall it's been a very solid and enjoyable playthrough for me. Plus it also had the benefit that I knew very little about it, compared to DS1, for which I saw plenty of footage from various areas, basically having a lot of the content spoiled for me.

There is the caveat that I have only finished the main campaign, and haven't started any of the 3 expansions. Which I hear are massive in size, probably close to the main campaign itself. But I'd been so immersed in FromSoft games lately, that I'm very close to being burned out. Though I would like to note down some remarks about it, so far, since I'm likely to forget some of the current context. And after this I do need to take a break before attempting the rest of the DS2 content. I guess too much of a good thing can be bad. Plus, the constant stress of these games surely can't be good for a long time. And it's been a pretty consistent emotional roller-coaster with this as, as was with DS1. I'll update this review after clearing the DLC content.

In terms of mechanics, I think I probably enjoyed the slight deviation in DS2 over DS1, or maybe it's just that it's the more recent experience. Overall combat is still as tight, responsive and rewarding as it was in DS1, but in part 2 they do expose more stats (ex, ADP) that you can control to make your character more to your liking. And I also particularly liked what they did with not allowing you to trigger attack swings when you don't have the stamina. In DS1 they used a sort of command queuing, so actions triggered when the character couldn't do them would queue up, and be performed on the next opportunity. This had the unfortunate effect of constantly having your character do something later than when you actually needed it. They seemed to have done away with this in DS2, and if you spam actions your character will not do anything. Which forces you to learn to pace your actions. And be attentive to your stamina bar.

World and level design is generally still good in this one, and while the level design is still solid, with plenty of stuff to explore, hidden areas and all that, the world design is significantly different to DS1. DS2's world is much more sprawling, and you very rarely return to previous areas. And as is probably well known by now, DS1 is much more interconnected and constantly winds down on itself, making exploration that much more intimate and meaningful. Plus, the first half of DS1 you play without the ability to teleport between bonfires, thus forcing you to learn the world that much more, and contend with the difficult areas a lot more. That is a feature that sadly probably wouldn't work as well in this one, but it's something I do miss none-the-less.

But even so, exploration and combat were still the best parts of this game. Making slow methodical progress in multiple directions and finding all the cleverly placed items throughout the world was still as fun as ever. And they're still as courageous as ever with level design, even hiding bonfires behind secret walls. Some of which I couldn't find on my own, had I not had a guide that I would consult after clearing an area to what I would call fully, and then still be surprised at the hidden stuff. Some of which you do wonder how exactly were found initially.

Generally, a lot of the positives and negatives of DS1 still apply, but I'm not sure I should rehash those any more. 

In terms of negatives, the only other one I could mention is the fact that, the world being so spread out some of the areas do seem like they weren't given as much attention as others. And some do feel downright empty and hastily put together. Unless that was an intentional design decision.

I also did feel some unevenness in terms of balancing, but the game being as complex as it is and punishing as it is, you're not really sure if something is intentional or not. I'll do say that the Iron Keep and the Giant visions were the areas where I got pounded into the ground the most, even after feeling somewhat overpowered before and in-between those two areas. And I keep hearing the DLC areas have some of the most punishing content. So I have that to look forward to.

The last significant positive, but maybe with some negative accents, was the change in how respawns work in DS2. I was surprised to find this out, but all enemies that usually endlessly respawn in DS1 were changed to a maximum count of 10 respawns in DS2. I hear this was to curb endless grinding. I did make great use of this new mechanic in one or two areas where I just couldn't have a consistent run to the area boss fight (looking at you Smelter Demon in Iron Keep). So I just buckled down and cleared that path 10 times, both gaining a good chunk of souls and making my path easier. Besides giving you an ultimate solution for particularly difficult areas this also helped reinforce the fact that souls were ultimately a limited resource, and easily exploitable enemies could only be exploited for a limited amount.

All in all a pretty solid experience with DS2, with plenty of grief and trolling from the developer. I think I'll remember the ambush by turtle knights that I suffered in the narrow corridor in Iron Keep for a long time. Not only did it take me a while to get through it, but then ultimately when I thought I was done they pulled off another troll on me right at the end. That stung a lot and plenty of expletives were thrown around. Not to detract too much from the other sections that pulled their own punches. But ultimately, that's one of the flavors that these games have that no other manages to pull off. A very intimate relationship, even bordering on Stockholm syndrome, with the game and the developers trying every which-way to screw with you. Not always pleasant but you do remember it for a long time. 

Update: In the mean time, after finishing the main campaign, but before getting too deep into the first expansion, I had restarted and replayed through the whole game with a dex-build using two rapiers in powerstance. A fantastic experience was had. So much more fun and even manageable than as a tank. 

After replaying it, I can honestly say I loved it even more than DS1. Though DS1 still has the better intertwined world design. You can't beat that. But in everything else, I loved DS2 considerably better. Of course, I'm also biased since a lot of the content in DS1 had been spoiled for me before getting to it, since it's so present everywhere.

So, an updated score: 9.2/10. Just so it's slightly ahead of DS1. :)

In comparison to the vanilla versions (x360 ps3 dx9), things have changed a lot. Areas have better and often more sensical/lore friendly enemy placements and the game feels a lot less empty. General progression is much more fluid in contrast to the game's general difficulty increase; vanilla may have been easier, but having to reach Iron Keep just to get the dull ember, or having to go through the Belfry Luna just to get the bastille key were a pain. In Scholar of the First Sin, these items exist in their appropriate areas.

I haven't finished Scholar just yet, but it already feels like the definitive version. General difficulty improvements and bug fixes are implemented from the get-go and the difficulty increase of the PvE experience never feels too over the top. There are more NPC summons in place to prevent people getting too stuck in certain areas after the game dies, NPCs appear in stranger places, sometimes more appropriate ones. A few hiccups remain from the conversion to 60fps, however, including some erratic movement from enemies that may attack far too quickly for you to parry, although capping your framerate somehow will fix these issues.

It still has the same problem Dark Souls 2 and 3 have - coming from the original Dark Souls, where poise was a gamekiller and parrying was almost a necessity, DS2 and 3 feel much easier and harder, allowing for viable dex builds and with less enemies having crazy amounts of poise, but parrying has been made a much more difficult and often pointless endeavour that is hard to drill out from your mind. The games went from a slow and clunky mess where parrying and poise breaking caused you to min/max and optimize, to a much more fluid game where dual wielding isn't awful and all weapons feel impactful, although some have their niche appeal. 

It's a hack and slash, now.

But after all that, it's still Dark Souls, just with a roll that isn't locked to four directions upon locking on, and with more friendliness towards fashion or whatever you specifically want to use, without the instant backstabs or the horrendous lag. People's main complaint come from the fact that it isn't a direct sequel. That's part of what makes DS2's story so great. To quote Arin Hanson of GameGrumps regarding these games: "You just go." That's precisely what DS2's story and level design is about. You aren't supposed to be clear on anything, not until the last second. Spend some time looking through the lore descriptions, listening to dialogue, or even just watching VaatiVidya's youtube videos and DS2 suddenly becomes an amazing evolution of the established Dark Souls plot, all hidden away under a shroud of player confusion and unclear goals.

"I believe they called it Drangleic. Perhaps you're familiar. No, how could you be. But one day, you will stand before its decrepit gate. Without really knowing why."

I don't wish to spoil much for DS2 newbies, but the plot being masked with a lack of information is both the game's strong point and its weakness. In DS1, you are given three distinct goals from a potential three different NPCs. In DS2 everything is vague; level design makes no sense and worlds seem to be connected together by dull, empty rooms with barely designed lifts that seem to shatter real-world physics, something often criticized by fans. But remember the epidemic of memory loss sweeping Drangleic? How would you remember how you really found yourself at your destination? All those dull, dark, empty, impossible and badly designed rooms are symbolic of the curse eating away at your memory, which is a strong focus of much of the game's story and characters. Nobody reliably remembers why they came or how they came. The symbolism simply compliments those barren rooms being necessary transitional/loading areas. It's amazing to me that all the prerequisites to truly understanding the story and the journey are given to you in the FIRST CUTSCENE OF THE GAME. 

Dark Souls 2 is a shining example of an underappreciated and fine sequel. Not bogging around in what was, no matter how great, but reimagining what was. A fresh new take on something you're already very familiar with, yet it suffered for the art. It doesn't have as many memorable moments in the base game as Dark Souls 1 did until the very end, whereas Dark Souls 1 had you venturing through painting worlds, falling through collapsed prisons and fighting remarkable bosses to great music, DS2's base game has a few decent bosses and gets much better as you access the DLC areas. Dark Souls 2 may not have as huge an impact on you as the first game did, but it certainly outclasses the first mechanically. You no longer have to be a tryhard to drive away invaders or stay hollowed for fear of constant OHKO invasions. It plays better, runs better, but being developed for the x360 and ps3 at the time, DS2 isn't going to leave your mouth agape too often.

This game is rather infamous as being the "black sheep" of the Fromsoft family, and because of that I only played this recently after having played all of the other Fromsoft titles. That being said, I believe that this game is worth a playthrough or two. It is bashed I think by the community too much, as it does a lot right, but at the same time is a bit deserving of its status. Let me explain:

For starters, this game is very different, and highly experimental. This is probably its greatest strength and weakness. Like powerstancing in Elden Ring? You can thank this game for bringing it to the series. Do you prefer a more open approach to progression as opposed to the linear nature of DS3 or Sekiro? This game gives you a surprising amount of freedom once you figure out the layout of the map. Enjoy build variety? There are so many different pieces of gear, armor, weapons, and spells to grind for. Whether its for a min/max PVP build or fashion souls there's something for everyone. Did you enjoy Int/Faith casting in another game? Again, thank DS2 for making it more mainstream (in the form of Hexes mainly). And as for Bonfire Ascetics, I really wish they had a similar mechanic to this in other games (Sekiro is the only one that came close with allowing you to re-fight bosses in a gauntlet). 

On the downside, this experimental approach can also lead to some very awful areas or encounters, easily some of the worst in the series, up there with Bed of Chaos. Black Gulch? I know that Miyazaki loves poison swamps, but this area is cancer. Snowfield in the 3rd DLC? Good luck and try not to lose your sanity; if you enjoy it then I'll certainly question yours. And as for boss design? There are some good ones, such as the community fan favorites of Sir Alonne or Fume Knight, and every Souls game has its fair share of weaker bosses, but fuck me there are a lot of fairly subpar boss encounters in this game (Skeleton Lords, Rat Vanguard, and Covetous Demon come to mind first).

Overall, its not a bad game, is underrated and I would recommend it. I had genuine fun trying out different builds and some of the unique spells and weapons are fun to play with. However, I wouldn't fault someone for disliking it and believe that you need to lower your expectations a bit when you go into this game, or you'll just end up getting frustrated and disappointed.

I did not get answers to all of these questions; but as I started exploring every nook and corner of the world I was slowly but surely getting a better understanding of the morbid world I had been banished to. That lack of purpose I had felt was swapped for a feeling of accomplishment as I started defeating the enemies in my path without much effort. Instead of wandering around an endless desert - I was now climbing a mountain reaching as far as you can imagine. 

This transition of feelings did not come easily though. For every accomplishment there were tenfold defeats that forced me to learn the attack patterns of my enemies - a skill that is necessary to both enjoy and complete any Dark Souls™ game. Overcoming difficult areas and bosses was both satisfying and rewarding - causing me to keep climbing that mountain in pursuit of purpose.

I started encountering more NPCs around the world. NPCs that told me tragic stories about their past. Stories about how they lost their family, how they were banished to this same world as me and branded with the accursed darksign. Some NPCs told me stories about their deepest fears and greatest wants, and I could relate to them in a way I rarely can with NPCs in a game. I wanted these NPCs to accomplish greatness and achieve their greatest wants. I wanted nothing but happiness for them, but this was not the case. Reality struck each one of them during our journeys and the fears they had told me about soon became true living nightmares. 

Wandering around aimlessly is dangerous for it is easy to lose grasp of what is what and who is who - or even why. [h1]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin review[/h1]
[i]Black sheep Souls[/i]

Widely considered to be the black sheep of the Souls family, [b][i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i][/b] is definitely the most divisive entry when it comes to the franchise. To be honest, I couldn't get along with this game for the longest time. Having adored the first entry (and generally loved everything FromSoftware has put out in recent years), the original [b][i]Dark Souls II[/i][/b] felt purposefully cumbersome to play, given how slow the original already was, which initially annoyed the hell out of me. It felt like playing the original [b][i]Dark Souls[/i][/b] but thickly draped in servings of molasses. The fact the game removed the ability to grind souls, each enemy now having a limited time they will respawn in the world before never spawning again, combined with an annoying health mechanic - where health is removed from the player each time the player dies unless they use a rare and valuable item to restore the health bar to its full capacity -  and some ropey, and downright questionable, hitboxes initially drove me nuts. It doesn't help that the game opens with some of the most dreadfully laboured starting zones that fail to pull the player into the adventure.

For many years [b][i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i][/b] remained that inaccessable entry in the series that I just couldn't get past. In 2021, and in preparation for [b][i]Elden Ring[/i][/b], I finally managed to build a bridge and get over myself and progress past my previous drop-off points, finally seeing the game to its conclusion (all DLC included) in single player. While I still don't think it's the best in the series (the original [b][i]Dark Souls[/i][/b] will forever hold that honor), and I do feel it's way to big and sprawling for its own good, by the end of my playthrough I could finally see why [b][i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i][/b] was so fiercely defended by a certain section of the fandom. The game certainly does get better, a whole lot better, once you progress past those first few lacklustre zones. It also happens to contain the best narrative in the series. It's a literal Shakeperian tragedy, with the game's plot taking a lot of narrative beats from Shakespeare's Macbeth, of a king wanting to do right by his kingdom but driven to madness and eventual grief by the very Queen who ruled by his side. Of course there is a lot more to it if you understand the [b][i]Dark Souls[/i][/b] universe and uncovering that through lore and conversations with NPC's is still part of the "souls-like" joy.

[b][i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i][/b] feels like that often misunderstood middle-child. Yes, it's a different beast from the Miyazaki directed first and third game, and one that we could argue is definitely the most jankiest, but it moved me more than the third adventure (which for a long time I felt was far superior). It features a dark, brooding, pervasively sad narrative (by now a staple of the series) with some of the best bosses to come out of the FromSoftware wheelhouse to date. [b][i]Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin[/i][/b] is hard won fight at the end of the day and while it may seem an unruly and messy experience at the start that offers little gratification, if given half the chance and accepted on its own terms you may finally find yourself being turned. Turned into a fan like me.

I got into the Souls Games early last year after playing Lies of Peak and then diving face first into the From Soft pc catalogue, going DS1, Sekiro, Elden Ring, DS3, then Nightreign, and all their DLCs (pour one for Seki-GOAT) before getting into this because of the horrific reputation it has as being the absolute worst in the series. In fact, I was originally never even planning on playing this game because everything I'd heard and seen about it seemed laughably bad. As if it took all of my least favorite things from the other From Soft games and slapped them into an absolute hair pulling abomination. But after beating DS3 and Nightreign I realized it'd be kinda dumb to actually have DS2 be the one and only From Soft game on PC that I never played, so I waited for it go on sale, and played it. And I gotta say, wow, the hate for this game is so undeserved it's actually insane.

[h1]TLDR[/h1]
This game is not perfect, but no Souls Game is. I love DS1, but I also must admit that it has some very jank hit boxes, the worst lock on in the series, and PGs and thieves will literally turn you around 180 degrees to back stab you. DS3 is no different, between the dogs, very little build variety due to the linear map design, and honestly, outside of the Grand Archives, probably my least favorite areas in all of From Soft. But they're still great games. If all you do is focus on the negatives, sure, they seem like ass, but DS1 still has probably the coolest map I've ever seen a video game, and DS3 has some of the best bosses in the series and completely changed how boss fights work in these games.
But DS2 just gets so much flak still, and I feel like it just comes from a lack of patience more than anything else. If you want to do nothing but book it from fog wall to fog wall in a makeshift boss rush then, yeah, go play DS3 or ER. But if you want to actually engage with the areas and the enemies in them, as I do, then this game is for you. The bosses aren't that amazing outside of a few, but the areas and world design more than make up for it to me (and that's coming from someone who puts boss fights typically before everything else in a video game), and while there are some areas and runbacks that are simply ass, when an area is good it is very good. Just don't run past enemies, bring a bow (or some form of range) to help kite for the mid to late game, get to 99 agility, grab the Ring of Binding, and you should be fine, and I hope you enjoy your run through Majula as much as I did!

That said, here's the detailed version of why people dislike this game and my experience with it.

[h1]Agility[/h1]
Agility is a stupid stat, I'm not even gonna pretend like it isn't. Basically, your i-frames in this game are not reliant on your character's equip load as much as it is a stat named Agility, which can be increased by upgrading your ADP. You need 99 agility to have the basic i-frames of a DS1 fastroll, which is the equivalent of having ~24ADP, which, given how easily you get souls in this game, I got to that threshold fairly quickly. So it's not really the issue people make it out to be, but it's not something I'm gonna pretend like I miss in the other games. Now for the real complaints.

[h1]Runbacks and Enemies[/h1]
This is why I had avoided this game. Because as much as I love DS1, I can't pretend like I don't absolutely despise some of the runbacks in that game, especially on my first playthrough when I was still learning some fights. And given how much people shit on this game for having some of the worst runbacks in the series, I was expecting a Gwyn level runback for essentially every boss, but honestly, a lot of the runbacks were more on par with say the Gargs: not particularly close, but definitely less of a walk than I was expecting. Also, this game isn't really well known for its challenging bosses, at least, not in the base game, and you will quickly notice that From Soft really made like 4 melee combos and went "yep, that'll do," and simply pasted that shit all over most of the enemies and bosses. So the runbacks, while they aren't great, they may not need to be traversed very many times, especially if you've already seen DS3 and beyond at this point like I have.

That said, when the runbacks ARE bad, ho-ly-fuck, they are [b]BAD![/b] So, let's talk enemy placement, the other major complaint I see all the time for DS2, but tbh, it's really not as bad as people make it out to be once you understand how the game works. Animations in this game are slow, very slow, and most actions, such as opening a door or even walking through a fog wall, all have some slow startup frames that do not give the player i-frames while they do it. So you can start going through the fog wall into a boss fight, only to then get smacked by an enemy you ran past otw there before you start actually traversing through it, knocking you out of the animation, and then all of the other enemies you ran past come and join the party and, yeah, back to the bonfire. Enemy leashes are also nigh infinite in this game, so good luck outrunning them, as most of the enemies in an area will, indeed, follow you to the ends of the Earth.

But, that's not to say it's that bad, IF you understand this going in and don't make the mistake of just running past every enemy you see. If you engage with the enemies one by one, most of them are absolute pushovers, and then you can peacefully enter that fog wall without any issues. I honestly quite enjoyed the areas because of this. It felt like doing a deathless run: just slowly but surely making my way through the game making sure not to aggro every enemy in an area at once. But that fun does go away the second you die at a boss with no bonfire closer than the one at the start of the area.

Old Iron Keep is probably the best example of this. Honestly a pretty fun area the first time through, imo, but when I got to that boss only for it to do some insane damage to me and send me all the way back to the beginning, yeah, the fun was over right then and there. I killed this boss in 3 tries, but I think it took me over an hour of my life all because of how slow I had to take it, because trust me, there is no getting into that fog gate with even a single enemy still hunting you, and there are a LOT of enemies.

But these style of runbacks were honestly few and far between, and there were even some where running past all of the enemies did indeed work, and when it didn't, once I knew the enemy placement, getting there wasn't that bad since I knew how to properly kite the enemies to me for quick 1v1s. And some areas just had no runbacks of any kind, very few, but it also did show me that this game is very fun when you only have to beat a level once. The first half of Iron Keep was a nightmare all because I died to the boss at the end and had to do it all over again from the start. But the second half had a bonfire right outside the boss's arena with just a single enemy between me and him, and that part I look back on fondly because it was fun, and I only had to do it once (and I, of course, first tried that boss... go figure).

[h]Still a Great Game[/h]
Now, after having finally played this game, while I understand the complaints people have of it, I also think this game is absolutely amazing. There are, I believe, 4 separate bosses that you can fight as your first boss realistically, but if you're willing to farm, you can add up to 5 more bosses to that list, and one is even a DLC boss, which is crazy! The open-ended-ness of this game is amazing to me, and the build variety is also spectacular. I get why people call Elden Ring DS2 2, they're not wrong, there's a lot of similarities between them. It's still not perfect, but damnit if I didn't love my run of this game, and I'm eager to get back into it for some challenge runs, because, much like ER, this really is a challenge runner's haven!

Dark Souls 2 SotFS clearly feels very different in style and atmosphere compared to the other games in the series. With this title, FromSoftware attempted to refresh the formula they had established in their previous games by introducing several new ideas. While some of these innovations successfully expanded and enriched the Souls formula, others unfortunately led to design decisions that caused Dark Souls II to gain a reputation as the “black sheep” of the series among parts of the community.

One of the most controversial mechanics is the health penalty on death. Each time you die, your maximum health decreases until you use a Human Effigy to restore your human form. After multiple deaths, your health can drop to nearly half of its maximum. While this penalty becomes less impactful later in the game, it can be quite punishing during the early stages when Human Effigies are limited.

Another issue is the heavy enemy density in many areas and the extremely long enemy aggro ranges. It often feels like enemies will chase you through nearly the entire zone, which strongly discourages the classic Souls strategy of running past enemies to reach the next checkpoint. It almost seems as if the developers intentionally wanted players to fight through every encounter.

Aside from these issues, Dark Souls II: Scholar of the First Sin is actually a significant step forward in several areas compared to Dark Souls. Combat variety is greater, NPC interactions are deeper, and the bosses and story presentation feel more cinematic overall. The atmosphere and soundtrack are also fantastic—especially when you first arrive at Majula. The calm and melancholic Majula theme that greets you and accompanies you throughout the game, along with many of the boss soundtracks, is a feast for the ears.

However, this positive momentum unfortunately lasts mainly until Iron Keep. After that point—especially with areas like Shrine of Amana—the game begins to amplify the previously mentioned frustrations, turning some sections into a rather irritating experience.

Despite these problems, I still enjoyed Dark Souls 2 more than many modern games that try to imitate the Souls-like formula. Contrary to what some people online suggest, this is definitely not a game that should be skipped when playing through the Souls series.

The Bonfire Ascetic system, which sadly never returned in later entries, is an excellent mechanic that allows players to essentially increase the difficulty of specific areas and refight bosses. The system involving petrified NPCs and enemies—where you choose who to free and when—also gives players meaningful control over progression and storytelling. In fact, the NPC questlines in this game are some of the best in the entire series.

While it certainly has areas where it could have been improved, Dark Souls 2 is still a fantastic Souls experience overall. I would strongly recommend it to anyone who enjoys the genre and wants to see how the series evolved over time.

So, to start off, I wanna say that i started out as a Dark Souls 3 player that sunk over 400 hours into that game before I decided to stop playing it and start playing the previous two games, Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls 2. Dark Souls 2 was the last entry in the series that I played, and it was a truly unique journey for me unlike anything Dark Souls 1 and Dark Souls 3 gave me. Here, I'll try listing the things I liked and didn't like about the game and you can come to your own conclusion on whether or not to buy it (duh). Also by the way, I do not recommend playing the trilogy in backwards order because DS3 can give you a lot of bad habits that'll make you suffer in the other two games.


Here's the things I liked:

The game has a LOT of content. One of my biggest complaints about DS1 and even DS3 was that it didn't have enough; I wanted more, and DS2 really did give me more. 

- The game has a truly large number of locations.
- An absolutely fantastic variety in color palette across all the locations.
- The game gives you multiple paths that you go through right from the start just like in DS1.
- The levels are for the most part more well thought-out than its prequel.
- The game has a sequel-worthy number of armors, weapons, spells, and items.
- A FANTASTIC variety of VIABLE builds.
- A great deal of quality-of-life improvements over DS1 such as the ATN (attunement) stat granting increased casting speed, increased spell uses, and increased attunement slots- all in one stat finally!
- Many mechanics that actually innovate and make it an overall large improvement over DS1 (more than it seems). 
- Hollowing is an actual mechanic that's surprisingly done pretty well and thankfully there's multiple ways of making it less annoying if the player wishes to do so.
- Durability is finally a proper mechanic that's more than just mere boss weapon ammo.
- DS1's issue of players being able to run past enemies largely without consequences is resolved by making enemies persistent.
- Great and interesting lore that's about drangleic and the various kingdoms that have come before it and the effects of hollowing for humans.
- Great story along with two of the most well-written characters in the trilogy who-shall-not-be-named-cus-it's-spoilers, and the best ending that one will ever see in the trilogy (it's the alternate ending).
- The game has a consistent level of quality throughout the vast majority of its content and doesn't fall off halfway like how  it did for DS1.
- Contrary to popular belief, the game actually overall has the tightest and most well-done hitboxes in the trilogy; the bad hitboxes problem is largely a myth.
- You can invade people regardless if they're hollow or not, and can disable invasions by burning a human effigy if you want.
- The game has the most balanced PvP experience.
- No shitty invasion priority system (fuck you for that, DS3!).
- The combat requires more thought from the player.
- Successive rolls have a greater stamina cost.
- The LEVELS LEADING UP TO THE BOSSES are more of a challenge than the vast majority bosses themselves, meaning the devs put a greater priority on the actual meat of the game.
- The game has among the best DLC's in the trilogy.
- The game has lots of subtle charm and detail that they absolutely did not need to go through the effort to make, but I'm glad they did, such as your character huffing when you're low on stamina.
- And finally the game ACTUALLY DOES A LOT TO ITS NG+ such as more items, new items, more enemies, new enemies, some bosses get some changes, a new boss encounter, and new NG+ exclusive lore.

Many people like praising the addition the powerstance mechanic but I think the addition that is even more praise-worthy is the inclusion of proper dual-wielding that is never seen ever again after DS2; being able to have a weapon's full moveset in both the right AND left hand is a wonderful thing and I don't understand why it never returned. Oh and your left hand no longer holds all left hand weapons as if they're straight swords.


Here's the things I didn't like:

Right away I will tell you that you will not see "ganks" and "a million enemies" in this list, because those are not flaws of this game; it's not as bad as people make it seem if you actually think things through.

- Too many healing items. I especially dislike that Melentia sells an unlimited number of lifegems at such a low cost so early into the game.
- ADP. I do like this stat for its ability to make heavy-weight builds more viable, and while it IS [i]somewhat[/i] communicated as to what it does in the stats menu, I still believe that it was not communicated well enough to the player as to what it does because this singular stat ON ITS OWN is responsible for all the false "bad hitboxes" claims that this game has received.
- Illusory walls (excluding Pharros walls) requiring you to press the interact button to uncover. The game makes NO effort to tell you how to uncover such walls, and I believe that DS1 and DS3's method of uncovering illusory walls is far more practical for a new player to figure out on their own.
- No password matchmaking for co-op.
- Soul Memory as a matchmaking system while a pretty neat idea, is awfully executed.
- The world isn't interconnected like how it was in DS1.
- A lot of level transitions don't make sense, although you could try explaining them by saying that they accurately follow one of the game's core themes.
- Some of the really cool levels are too short (this is personal nitpick).
- The vast majority of the base game bosses SUCK!
- The easiest-to-get ending sucks.
- The first half of Iron Keep is terrible if you're a new player that's trying to do the boss runback for that part of the location. (tip: wear armor with actual poise and jump onto the platform just before the bridge for a shorter runback). I've no idea why they couldn't just rework that first half for Scholar of the First Sin's release!
- The lighting isn't as atmospheric as DS1, although this is a personal taste thing.


This game has been an incredible journey for me and despite its flaws I still really enjoy it. I'm super sad that we will most likely never get a game like this again, as it seems that FromSoftware and Soulslikes in general are more interested in making speedy games nowadays and also there being no sign that Yui Tanimura (the creator of DS2) is interested in making another game, which is sad because I believe he's capable of making great games based on the overall quality of DS2 and the DLC's he's directed for this game and the fact that he somehow saved the game from being an entirely unplayable mess in less than a year after taking over mid-development; I'm glad he's been Miyazaki's co-director ever since, though! Good for him!
