If you're checking in to see if Dark Souls in general is the kind of game you'd like, you're better off reading the far more comprehensive review of Dark Souls 1, which can be found here: https://steamcommunity.com/id/ninthbelief/recommended/211420/

As with the original Dark Souls, there are two caveats that must be prefaced when reviewing Dark Souls 2. 

First, you must have a controller available to play this game, as the style of game Dark Souls is cannot be properly enjoyed on a keyboard and mouse setup, and that would be even if the controls were stellar on the KB+M, which they are not.

Second, the game has two editions: “vanilla” DS2 and Scholar of the First Sin. You want to buy Scholar of the First Sin, as even though it’s significantly harder, there are many improvements to the game and more imporantly the DLC is entirely bundled and naturalized within SotFS (as opposed to spawning with keys in the vanilla edition).

A third, additional caveat here is that yes, you should play Dark Souls 1 first -- the Remastered Edition requires far less setup than the original, so if you have to choose, stick with the Remastered Edition. The story for the trilogy is one of the best ever told, and you're missing massive parts that hit hard if you're skipping around the games instead of playing them in order.

On with the review.

There is a suspicion among fans of FromSoftware that Miyazaki hates sequels, spurred on by non-existent quotes of him supposedly saying as much. Such an interview never existed, such thoughts have never been publicized.

However, if you were to believe this line of thinking, you wouldn’t be surprised by the nature of Dark Souls 2; the game isn’t, on the surface, a traditional sequel in any capacity. It starts by distancing itself thousands of years after the original Dark Souls, and there are close to zero recognizable characters of any sort in the entire game. 

What is traditional for this sequel, in line with video game sequels specifically, is that there are an absurd amounts of steps “forward” – I put that word in quotations because if you’ve played a video game sequel before, you know there’s no truer use of the idiom “you don’t make an omelet without breaking a few eggs”. Video game sequels often try to innovate, and innovation requires thinking that isn’t strictly forward. You can then take the feedback from your first two games contrasted against each other for a "perfect" third game (behold, Halo 3). 

This has led to numerous changes from its predecessor that divide the community; I would say that even the distanced story is one of those intentional changes, and adds a ton of contrast to the series as a whole.

But, the bottom line: does Dark Souls 2 succeed as a game overall? Is it entertaining? Would fans of Dark Souls 1 or Dark Souls 3 enjoy the game?

Absolutely, emphatically yes. Across the board.

Of the community’s critiques for Dark Souls 2, most of them ring the exact same as the “Wooow, nothing I could do” crowd of beginners in DS1 who never crawled out of the Burg. That isn’t to say they’re terrible or that they’re terrible people, just that they fell for the same familiar trappings that came with the original game, but the idea is that they’re somehow worse because they “aren’t the same as Dark Souls 1.”

The two you’ll hear most commonly are that “the game is just so clunky, sigh” (sound familiar?) and “roll iframes being tied to a stat is dumb and unexplained”. (Again, sound familiar?)

Any time someone dies in a Souls game, the first thing they’ll try to squeeze the failure on is a self described clunky control scheme, and they’ll cite things like “delays”. While this is understandable for a beginner who hasn’t gotten used to the idea that they cant attack and block at the same time, it’s a bit less charming coming from someone who was completely capable of completing any other FromSoftware game. If you’re watching them play, you’ll probably see the basic mistakes anyone makes (mistimed rolls, poor stamina management, failing to understand stamina penalties, and straight panic). The only sin that Dark Souls 2 adds on in this regard is that it’s not the exact same engine Dark Souls 1 uses, so there’s a small period of time spent finding your feet again before you’re back in killing shape.

As for the second critique, I think any observer familiar with DS1 mechanics will be in-the-know about iframes in DS1 – they were granted by your weight vs your weight limit, which was increased by END, and that too was “unexplained” within its own game. What people are actually critiquing is that the stat that increases your iframes directly is no longer the same one that affects your weight limit, it’s now adaptability or “ADP”. Whether you’re a veteran or a newcomer, you’re gonna wanna level up ADP to 25-30 or so and then you’re free to do whatever else you like. People have done the game with the bare minimum of ADP, so it’s not a mandatory stat or anything – it’s just a very, very good idea, especially if you want iframes to be your primary defensive tool or are used to DS1’s iframes.

A third, valid critique of DS2 is the Soul Memory system, which was put in place to stop experienced players from destroying new players; a problem that plagues the living hell out of DS1 and DS3. SM is an extreme system that measures how many souls you’ve picked up over the course of the entire game, and places you in a tier with players who’ve acquired a similar amount of souls. Important thing to note here – it’s not affected by how many souls you’ve spent, just how many you’ve picked up, which leads people to think that they’ve “wasted” their souls and “ruined” their character when they lose a soul stain. Obviously, since tiers are pretty big, you’d have to lose billions of souls for this to matter, but it doesn’t stop people from the feeling. 

The other important factor here is that it makes grouping with friends difficult, as the other FromSoftware games (all if you’re including DS1 remastered over the original DS1) use a password system alongside character scaling tech to make you able to play with your friends any time. Since this one is tiered by SM, while the range is increased when you’re looking for friends, you’re better off just making new characters together if you want to co-op. This makes some people antsy, but Dark Souls is far and away a better experience when played with no summons your first time through, so take from that what you will.

Those problems aside, you’ll find tons of excellent feel improvements over the original game – character creation has been immensely improved and characters themselves look significantly better, especially texture wise. “Powerstancing“, while it’s a complicated system, is a straight upgrade from DS1’s dual-wielding system – which is to say that it didn’t have one at all, off-hand weapons were forced as “shields” mechanically. In DS2, a broad variety of weapons can be wielded together for unique movesets, which is super rad, and a system that you’ll miss in Dark Souls 3. “Wizard hat” magic doesn’t get better than DS2, especially hexes which are their own spell category for this game and this game only. Graphics are improved across the board, beautiful cloth physics on capes and plumes included. 

Some of my favorite bosses and far and away my favorite story is within DS2 – it’s part of the bandwagon to hate the game within the community because it’s many, many steps in a direction away from DS1, but there is a fantastic game here that you should absolutely spend time with. I’d recommend it to anyone – and if you find it’s truly, deeply not your cup of tea even though you enjoyed DS1, you’ll find that DS3 treats this game like a red-headed step child and does it’s best to forget about it, improvements and all.
